docs.title: Absent rules and conditional gates migration (appVersion → next minor)
docs.text:
[!WARNING] 1.x only. This page describes repo-guardian 1.x. v2 has no equivalent: file checks are file controls, listed in the control-type reference.

IMPL-0019 adds a fourth file-rule check mode, check = "absent", whose remediation is a file-deletion PR, plus a when { rule_satisfied = "<rule>" } block that gates any file rule on a sibling rule being satisfied on the default branch (DESIGN-0020).

Absent-mode deletion is the engine's first destructive remediation. This guide leads with the dry-run recipe, then covers the operational edges an upgrading operator will hit. It is additive — existing policies with no absent rule and no when {} block behave exactly as before.

docs.title: 1. Dry-run first (do this before enabling)
docs.text:
Because an absent rule deletes files, validate the blast radius before letting it write. Set the engine to dry-run and inspect the logs:

# On the Deployment (env wins over HCL/defaults):
DRY_RUN=true

With dry_run = true an actionable absent rule logs its planned deletions and mutates nothing:

level=INFO msg="dry run: would create PR" actionable_rules=[no_dependabot] \
  planned_deletions=[.github/dependabot.yml]

Confirm the planned_deletions list matches what you expect across your fleet, then flip DRY_RUN=false (or remove the override) to let the removal PRs open.

docs.title: 2. Policy-hash bump → one full re-sweep
docs.text: Adding an absent rule or a when {} block changes the policy version hash (policy.Version). The stale-sweeper treats every repo_state row whose policy_version predates the change as drifted, so the first sweep after upgrade re-checks every repo. This is expected and self-limiting — subsequent sweeps return to steady state once rows are re-stamped. Expect a one-time spike in repos_checked_total and GitHub API usage; the per-installation rate-limit reserve and budget gate still apply, so the sweep paces itself.

docs.title: 3. Reconcile-log hash bump → one comment edit per open PR
docs.text: The sticky reconcile-log comment gained absent-aware and gate-closed status strings (present on main, pending removal, absent from main, skipped (when-gate closed: <referee> not satisfied)). These strings feed the comment's content hash, so every open repo-guardian PR gets exactly one extra comment edit on the first reconcile after upgrade, after which identical-state sweeps converge to zero edits again.

docs.title: 4. search_terms must not collide with the add-era PR
docs.text:
An absent rule's PR is discovered by the same pr.search_terms mechanism as add rules. If a no_dependabot absent rule reused search_terms = ["dependabot"], its removal PR would be mistaken for the old add PR and skipped. Give absent rules a distinct phrase:

rule "file" "no_dependabot" {
  check = "absent"
  paths = [".github/dependabot.yml", ".github/dependabot.yaml"]

  when {
    rule_satisfied = "renovate_config"
  }

  pr {
    search_terms = ["remove dependabot"]
    title        = "chore({{ .Repo }}): remove Dependabot config (repo uses Renovate)"
  }
}

docs.title: 5. Two-PR convergence is deliberate
docs.text: The gate reads the default branch only, so a repo that has Dependabot but not yet Renovate converges over two PR cycles: sweep 1 opens the add-Renovate PR (the gate is closed, so nothing is deleted); after a human merges it, a later sweep sees the gate open and opens the remove-Dependabot PR. repo-guardian never deletes Dependabot before Renovate is actually live and reviewed. Merging the Renovate PR triggers the gated re-check on the push path, so you don't wait for the next scheduled sweep.

docs.title: 6. Downgrade behavior — fails loud
docs.text: An older binary that predates absent mode rejects a policy containing check = "absent" at load with an "invalid check mode" error and refuses to start, rather than silently misinterpreting the rule. If you must roll back the binary, roll back the policy in the same change.

docs.title: Fail-safe recap
docs.text:
Every destructive step is fail-safe, mirroring the IMPL-0013 Q9 stance:

  • A gate evaluation error closes the gate (rule skipped), never opens it.
  • A file already gone from the reconcile branch is an idempotent skip.
  • Restoration of a no-longer-forbidden file (inverse orphan) and orphan cleanup both leave the path untouched on any API error, increment pr_orphan_left_total, and retry on the next sweep.

docs.title: Custom-property annotation migration (appVersion 1.9.1 → next minor)
docs.text:
[!WARNING] 1.x only. This page describes repo-guardian 1.x. v2 has no equivalent: custom properties are the custom_properties control type, in the control-type reference.

IMPL-0017 replaces the custom_properties reconciler's hardcoded Jira annotation extraction with an operator-defined annotation_properties map (DESIGN-0019). This is a roll-forward-only change: no deprecation window, no compatibility shim. It closes INV-0008.

This guide walks through the four behavioral edges an upgrading operator may hit.

docs.title: 1. Built-in Jira extraction is gone
docs.text:
Before this change, catalog.Parse always looked for jira/project-key and jira/label annotations and populated JiraProject/JiraLabel custom properties — with no way to configure, rename, or disable that behavior. It now extracts nothing beyond the two Backstage-contract-guaranteed fields (Owner ← spec.owner, Component ← metadata.name) unless you opt in:

reconcile "custom_properties" {
  mode = "api"
  annotation_properties = {
    "jira/project-key" = "JiraProject"
    "jira/label"        = "JiraLabel"
  }
}

If your policy relied on the old built-in behavior and doesn't declare this map, JiraProject/JiraLabel simply stop being synced — no error, no warning, because as far as repo-guardian is concerned they're no longer in the managed set. Add the map above (or map whatever annotations/properties you actually use) to restore the old behavior. See docs/usage/policy-reference.md § custom_properties for the full attribute reference and validation rules.

docs.title: 2. Template context: .Catalog.Jira* is gone
docs.text:
If any custom PR/file template referenced the old fields directly, rewrite them:

Before After {{ .Catalog.JiraProject }} {{ index .Catalog.Properties "JiraProject" }} {{ .Catalog.JiraLabel }} {{ index .Catalog.Properties "JiraLabel" }}

.Catalog.Properties is a map[string]string keyed by the GitHub property name (the map's values in annotation_properties, not its keys). Every mapped property is present in the map — an absent source annotation renders as an empty string (the same "will clear" signal the embedded set-custom-properties.tmpl workflow uses), so {{ if index .Catalog.Properties "JiraProject" }} is the idiomatic guard if you want to skip rendering a line entirely rather than render it empty. .Catalog.Owner and .Catalog.Component are unchanged.

docs.title: 3. Removed annotations now clear the property (full state sync)
docs.text:
Previously, once a Jira property was set on a repo it stayed set even if the annotation was later removed from catalog-info.yaml — there was no mechanism to un-set it. annotation_properties targets are now a full state sync: add, update, and clear. If a mapped annotation disappears (edited out, or the whole file removed), the corresponding GitHub property is set to null on the next reconcile.

Note (IMPL-0021). Only the edited-out annotation half of this worked when it first shipped. The whole file removed half was unreachable — the engine skipped reconcilers entirely when the file was missing, so a deleted catalog-info.yaml left every mapped property stale (INV-0011 A3). Both halves behave as documented from appVersion 1.10.1 on. When the file is gone, Owner/Component fall back to Unclassified rather than clearing.

If you were relying on the old "sticky" behavior (a property, once set, persists even after the source annotation is removed), there is no opt-out — this is the DESIGN-0019 resolution (OQ 3 → b) and is considered a correctness fix, not a new footgun: a stale, no-longer-true property value is worse than a cleared one. Re-add the annotation if you want the value back.

docs.title: 4. Optional new App permission: org-level "Custom properties: read"
docs.text:
Phase 3 adds a schema preflight: before writing, repo-guardian checks which custom properties the org's schema actually defines and drops any mapped property the schema doesn't have, so one undefined property doesn't block the rest of the sync. This is optional and fails open:

  • Without the permission (or on any schema-endpoint error): every managed property syncs exactly as it did before this release — the unfiltered payload is sent, once per org per 30-minute window a slog.Warn line notes the schema fetch failed (see docs/operations/scaling.md § Custom-property schema preflight for the exact log text). No action required.
  • With the permission granted: a mapped property with no matching org-schema definition is dropped from the PATCH (the rest still syncs), logged, and counted via repo_guardian_custom_property_missing_schema_total{org, property}. Define the property in the org's custom-property schema (GitHub settings, not repo-guardian — the App never creates schema itself) to make the warning go away.

Granting the permission is a strict improvement in visibility with no behavior change for repos whose schema is already correct. There is no reason to grant it except to get the preflight warning/metric; declining it reproduces pre-Phase-3 behavior indefinitely.

docs.title: Validation steps
docs.text:
1. Diff your policy against the table above — do you reference .Catalog.Jira* anywhere, or rely on the old hardcoded Jira extraction without declaring annotation_properties?
  2. Dry-run: set DRY_RUN=true (or guardian { dry_run = true }) and check the logs for "custom properties need update" — the desired_properties field shows exactly what would sync under the new map-driven behavior.
  3. If you want the schema preflight, grant the App org-level "Custom properties: read" permission and confirm repo_guardian_custom_property_missing_schema_total stays at zero (or investigate the named property if it doesn't).

docs.title: Rollback
docs.text: Roll-forward only — there is no compatibility shim to fall back to. If a rollback is needed, pin the binary/chart to the previous appVersion; the old hardcoded Jira behavior returns, but any properties cleared under the new full-state-sync behavior are not automatically restored (GitHub still shows them as unset until the old binary's next successful sync re-sets them from catalog-info).

docs.text:

  • DESIGN-0019 — design rationale
  • INV-0008 — investigation that motivated this change
  • docs/usage/policy-reference.md — operator-facing attribute reference
  • docs/operations/scaling.md — schema-preflight metrics + Loki matching contract

docs.title: Running repo-guardian on AWS
docs.text:
How to run repo-guardian v2 on EKS with the AWS-managed pieces around it: RDS or Aurora for Postgres, Secrets Manager and the External Secrets Operator (ESO) for credentials, and an AWS load balancer for the webhook route. Nothing in the binary is AWS-aware. The work is in provisioning the managed services and getting their credentials into Kubernetes Secrets that the chart references.

Read Turning on repo-guardian v2 first. This page covers only what is different on AWS. Scaling repo-guardian covers sizing.

If you provision with libtftest-tf-modules/modules/rds/*, the variable-level companion to this page is External Postgres on RDS — Terraform variable reference: settings for instance / cluster / serverless, each with and without proxy.

[!NOTE] Valkey (and ElastiCache with it) was removed in v2. There is no queue or scheduler backend: Temporal holds every workflow, timer and schedule. If you are coming from 1.x, delete the ElastiCache cluster once the cutover in Moving to repo-guardian v2 is done.

docs.title: What runs where
docs.text: Piece On AWS Owned by ingest, evaluator, remediator, api, ui EKS, one Deployment per role (topology: split) this chart Postgres (the controls database) RDS for PostgreSQL or Aurora PostgreSQL, ideally behind RDS Proxy you Temporal Temporal Cloud, or a self-hosted cluster (for example on EKS with its own RDS database) you Credentials Secrets Manager, synced into Kubernetes Secrets by ESO you Webhook route an ALB or NLB through the AWS Load Balancer Controller you Images and chart GHCR (public), or the private ECR mirror maintainers publish, you pull

docs.title: Temporal
docs.text:
Temporal is required and is not part of this chart. repo-guardian is a client of it: the workers dial the frontend, nothing more. Running Temporal (its own persistence database, upgrades, retention) is the operator's job, the same way the database is.

What repo-guardian needs from it is listed in 2. A Temporal cluster: server 1.31 or newer, a namespace, reachability on port 7233 from the repo-guardian namespace, and mTLS or OIDC credentials. On AWS that usually means one more security-group rule (EKS nodes to the Temporal frontend) and one more Secret.

KEDA's default trigger reads the Temporal server's approximate_backlog_count from Prometheus. If your Prometheus does not scrape the Temporal server (a managed Temporal, for example), use keda.trigger: temporal with mTLS, or set evaluator.keda.query / remediator.keda.query to a query your metrics can answer. See Autoscaling with KEDA. For Amazon Managed Service for Prometheus, point keda.prometheus.serverAddress at its query endpoint and name your SigV4 TriggerAuthentication in keda.prometheus.authenticationRef.

docs.title: Option matrix
docs.text:
Service Best for Notes RDS for PostgreSQL (provisioned) Predictable steady-state load Cheapest per hour for a known load. Manual instance-class sizing. Multi-AZ for HA. Aurora Serverless v2 Spiky or idle load ACU-based scaling. repo-guardian is mostly idle between evaluations, which suits it, but only with RDS Proxy in front. Aurora PostgreSQL (provisioned) HA and read scaling Separate writer and reader endpoints. The api role's read-only DSN can use the reader endpoint (see Reader endpoint for the API).

All three speak plain Postgres, so internal/store/postgres works unchanged. The decision is operational, not architectural.

Version and parameter parity with the chart. The chart's two managed shapes both pin Postgres 18 (store.postgres.baked.image: postgres:18.4, store.postgres.cnpg.imageName: ...postgresql:18.4). Pin the RDS engine_version to the same major so dev and test on the chart-managed shapes run the major production runs. Neither chart mode sets custom Postgres parameters, so default parameter groups are correct. Details: Parameter groups and engine version.

The database must be empty before the first migration: the controls schema chain refuses a database that already holds an older schema.

docs.title: Database users
docs.text:
v2 does not connect as one user. Column-level grants are the boundary between the evaluator and the remediator, so each role gets its own login. Migrations grant to these users and never create them, so on RDS you create them yourself, before the first helm install.

User Used by Secret (chart value) Env var in the pod rg_owner the migrate Job only: owns the schema, runs repo-guardian migrate store.postgres.existingSecret STORE_DSN rg_evaluator evaluator pods store.controls.evaluator.existingSecret STORE_DSN_EVALUATOR rg_remediator remediator pods store.controls.remediator.existingSecret STORE_DSN_REMEDIATOR rg_all topology: all pods only (a member of both roles above) store.controls.all.existingSecret both of the above a read-only login, here rg_api_ro api pods api.roDsn.existingSecret STORE_RO_DSN

The chart-managed shapes (baked, cnpg) create the same users for you, and call the read-only one repoguardian_ro. On external the names are yours; only the grants matter.

As the RDS master user, before the first install:

-- The owner. Not a superuser, so the grants the migrations write bind.
CREATE ROLE rg_owner LOGIN PASSWORD '...' NOSUPERUSER NOCREATEROLE;
GRANT ALL ON SCHEMA public TO rg_owner;

-- The application users.
CREATE ROLE rg_evaluator  LOGIN PASSWORD '...' NOSUPERUSER;
CREATE ROLE rg_remediator LOGIN PASSWORD '...' NOSUPERUSER;
GRANT USAGE ON SCHEMA public TO rg_evaluator, rg_remediator;
-- Only for topology: all.
-- CREATE ROLE rg_all LOGIN PASSWORD '...' NOSUPERUSER IN ROLE rg_evaluator, rg_remediator;

-- The API's read-only login.
CREATE ROLE rg_api_ro LOGIN PASSWORD '...' NOSUPERUSER;
GRANT CONNECT ON DATABASE repoguardian TO rg_api_ro;
GRANT USAGE ON SCHEMA public TO rg_api_ro;

Then, connected as rg_owner, give the read-only login every table the migrations create now and later:

ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES IN SCHEMA public GRANT SELECT ON TABLES TO rg_api_ro;
GRANT SELECT ON ALL TABLES IN SCHEMA public TO rg_api_ro;

The row-level-security read policies on the controls tables are PUBLIC, so plain SELECT is enough for the API to see every row. Change repoguardian to your database_name.

docs.title: Chart values for external Postgres
docs.text:
store:
  postgres:
    mode: external
    existingSecret: repo-guardian-db-owner          # rg_owner; the migrate Job
    existingSecretKey: STORE_DSN
  controls:
    enabled: true                                   # per-role users; off by default
    evaluator:
      existingSecret: repo-guardian-db-evaluator
      existingSecretKey: STORE_DSN_EVALUATOR
    remediator:
      existingSecret: repo-guardian-db-remediator
      existingSecretKey: STORE_DSN_REMEDIATOR

api:
  enabled: true
  roDsn:
    existingSecret: repo-guardian-db-ro             # required on external with split + api
    existingSecretKey: STORE_RO_DSN

With store.controls.enabled: true, a split evaluator or remediator pod gets only its own DSN and no STORE_DSN; only the migrate Job keeps the owner's credentials. With it off, every controls pod falls back to STORE_DSN, which on RDS means the workers run as the owner. Turn it on.

The chart refuses to render when a needed Secret is missing: store.controls.evaluator.existingSecret while github.eval.appId is set, store.controls.remediator.existingSecret while github.remediate.appId is set (store.controls.all.existingSecret under topology: all), and any store.controls.*.existingSecret set outside mode: external.

Each controls worker logs which DSN it used at startup (dsn_env and db_user on the "controls store" line). Check it after the first deploy.

docs.title: Credentials via External Secrets Operator
docs.text:
Keep one Secrets Manager secret per database user, and one ESO ExternalSecret per Kubernetes Secret. RDS Proxy needs a Secrets Manager secret per user anyway, and a pod then can only ever be handed its own credentials.

Secrets Manager: rds/repo-guardian/evaluator
   ↓ ESO ExternalSecret
k8s Secret repo-guardian-db-evaluator (key STORE_DSN_EVALUATOR)
   ↓ store.controls.evaluator.existingSecret
evaluator pods

Example for the evaluator; repeat it for the owner (STORE_DSN), the remediator (STORE_DSN_REMEDIATOR) and the API (STORE_RO_DSN):

apiVersion: external-secrets.io/v1beta1
kind: ExternalSecret
metadata:
  name: repo-guardian-db-evaluator
  namespace: repo-guardian
spec:
  refreshInterval: 1h
  secretStoreRef:
    name: aws-secrets-manager
    kind: ClusterSecretStore
  target:
    name: repo-guardian-db-evaluator
    template:
      data:
        # urlquery percent-encodes reserved characters; the replace
        # re-maps space from "+" (query-string form) to %20 (userinfo
        # form). Without this, a password containing @ : / % or space
        # produces a DSN that fails to parse or authenticates with the
        # wrong password. ESO templates are Go text/template + Sprig,
        # so both functions are available.
        STORE_DSN_EVALUATOR: "postgres://{{ .username }}:{{ .password | urlquery | replace \"+\" \"%20\" }}@{{ .endpoint }}:5432/{{ .dbname }}?sslmode=require"
  data:
    - secretKey: username
      remoteRef:
        key: rds/repo-guardian/evaluator
        property: username
    - secretKey: password
      remoteRef:
        key: rds/repo-guardian/evaluator
        property: password
    - secretKey: endpoint
      remoteRef:
        key: rds/repo-guardian/evaluator
        property: endpoint
    - secretKey: dbname
      remoteRef:
        key: rds/repo-guardian/evaluator
        property: dbname

Point the worker DSNs at the RDS Proxy endpoint. The owner and API DSNs can point elsewhere (below). Why the encoding matters, and how a mis-encoded password fails: Building the DSN.

docs.title: Connection pooling: RDS Proxy
docs.text:
Put RDS Proxy in front of any of the three Postgres variants for the evaluator and remediator:

  • It survives instance failovers without dropping client connections.
  • It absorbs the reconnect burst when a KEDA scale-out or a rollout starts several pods at once.
  • It is close to required with Serverless v2, where scaling events otherwise drop connections.
  • It adds a few milliseconds per round trip, which does not matter at repo-guardian's query rate.

Register a Secrets Manager secret for each user that connects through the proxy (rg_evaluator, rg_remediator). Size the proxy's max_connections_percent to the sum of the worker pools; the math is in Connection math.

Two DSNs do not need the proxy:

  • The owner (STORE_DSN) is used only by the migrate Job, a few times per release. Goose holds a session-level advisory lock while it migrates, which pins a proxy connection for the duration. That is harmless, but with store.controls.enabled the owner DSN is its own Secret, so you can point it at the instance or cluster endpoint directly and skip the proxy.
  • The API (STORE_RO_DSN) sets default_transaction_read_only and a 5s statement_timeout on every new session. Those SETs pin each connection to the proxy (at most 8 per api replica). Point it at the database or a reader endpoint directly instead.

docs.title: Reader endpoint for the API
docs.text: The api role opens its own pool (8 connections per replica) on STORE_RO_DSN, runs every read in a read-only transaction, and writes nothing. On Aurora you can point api.roDsn at the reader endpoint to keep dashboard and UI traffic off the writer. The workers must stay on the writer: they write on every evaluation and remediation.

docs.title: Gaps and workarounds
docs.text:
• No IAM database authentication. The pools are built from static DSNs with no per-connection token hook, and IAM tokens expire after 15 minutes. Use password auth through Secrets Manager. RDS Proxy can still use IAM between the proxy and the database.
  • Password rotation is not transparent. A pod reads its DSN from the environment at start. When Secrets Manager rotates a password and ESO re-syncs the Kubernetes Secret, open connections keep working until they are recycled, but new ones fail until the pod restarts. RDS Proxy does not remove this: clients authenticate to the proxy with the same credentials it holds. Automate a rollout on Secret change (a reloader-style annotation), or rotate on your own schedule. Each user rotates separately, so only that role's pods restart.

docs.title: Webhook route
docs.text: The chart ships no webhook Ingress. On EKS, the AWS Load Balancer Controller with the Gateway API is the documented option: AWS LBC + Gateway API (EKS). Route both App paths, /webhooks/github/eval and /webhooks/github/remediate, to the ingest Service. If you want to restrict source IPs to GitHub's hook ranges, do it on the load balancer: the app checks only the HMAC signature.

docs.title: Images, ECR and IAM
docs.text:
The public images and chart are on GHCR. Maintainers also publish to a private ECR mirror (repo-guardian for the image, repo-guardian-chart for the chart); pulling from it needs ECR read on the node role or the pull identity. See Consumer-side install.

The repo-guardian pods need no AWS permissions: they speak Postgres, Temporal and the GitHub API. The IAM role (IRSA or EKS Pod Identity) belongs to ESO's ServiceAccount, with secretsmanager:GetSecretValue on the repo-guardian secrets listed below. Leave serviceAccount.annotations empty unless something else in your cluster needs it.

docs.title: One busy organisation
docs.text:
At enterprise scale the question is what happens when one large organisation has far more work than the rest. In v2 it is answered by the rate budget, not by the infrastructure:

  • Each App's installation has its own budget workflow, installation/eval/<installation id> and installation/remediate/<installation id>, tracking that installation's GitHub rate limit. A busy organisation that exhausts its budget makes its own evaluations wait for its own reset. It cannot spend another organisation's budget.
  • A waiting evaluation is a durable Temporal timer, not a held worker slot, so other installations' work keeps flowing through the same pods.
  • Every activity and workflow start carries the installation id as its Temporal fairness key.

There is no queue to partition and nothing to shard. The levers that remain are the ones in The GitHub rate budget.

docs.title: End-to-end example
docs.text:
Values for a fleet of a few thousand repositories across tens of GitHub Enterprise Cloud organisations, with remediation on:

topology: split

temporal:
  address: temporal-frontend.temporal.svc:7233
  namespace: repo-guardian
  tls:
    existingSecret: repo-guardian-temporal-mtls

github:
  eval:
    appId: "123456"
    existingSecret: rg-eval-app            # private-key, webhook-secret
  remediate:
    appId: "234567"
    existingSecret: rg-remediate-app

ingest:
  replicas: 2

evaluator:
  concurrency: 10
  dbPoolSize: 12
  keda:
    enabled: true
    minReplicas: 1
    maxReplicas: 4

remediator:
  concurrency: 10
  dbPoolSize: 0                            # concurrency + 4 = 14
  keda:
    enabled: true
    minReplicas: 0
    maxReplicas: 2

keda:
  trigger: prometheus
  prometheus:
    serverAddress: http://prometheus.monitoring:9090

store:
  postgres:
    mode: external
    existingSecret: repo-guardian-db-owner
  controls:
    enabled: true
    evaluator:
      existingSecret: repo-guardian-db-evaluator
    remediator:
      existingSecret: repo-guardian-db-remediator

api:
  enabled: true
  replicas: 2
  roDsn:
    existingSecret: repo-guardian-db-ro
  auth:
    issuer: https://idp.example.com/realms/platform

# plus policy.files (or policy.existingConfigMap): see v2-onboarding.md

Companion AWS resources:

Resource Purpose Sizing Aurora PostgreSQL cluster (or RDS for PostgreSQL, Multi-AZ) The controls database db.r6g.large writer + 1 reader; storage auto-scaling RDS Proxy Pool for the evaluator and remediator Fronts the writer; one auth secret per worker user; max_connections_percent 50–75 Secrets Manager: rds/repo-guardian/{owner,evaluator,remediator,api-ro} One secret per database user Rotation on your schedule, see above Secrets Manager: the two App keys and webhook secrets rg-eval-app, rg-remediate-app Keys rotate by adding a second key on the App registration ESO ClusterSecretStore aws-secrets-manager Secrets Manager to Kubernetes IRSA or Pod Identity on ESO's ServiceAccount Temporal Workflows, timers, schedules Yours: Temporal Cloud, or self-hosted with its own database EKS namespace repo-guardian Pod placement Private subnets; egress to api.github.com and the Temporal frontend ALB or NLB via the AWS Load Balancer Controller Webhook route to ingest Optionally restricted to GitHub's hook ranges VPC endpoints Secrets Manager, STS, ECR Optional; cut NAT cost at scale

Security-group rules:

  • EKS nodes → RDS Proxy on 5432 (evaluator, remediator)
  • EKS nodes → the database writer on 5432 (migrate Job, if it skips the proxy)
  • EKS nodes → the reader endpoint on 5432 (api, if it uses the reader)
  • RDS Proxy → the database on 5432
  • EKS nodes → the Temporal frontend on 7233

docs.title: Chart 0.5.0 migration runbook (IMPL-0011)
docs.text:
[!WARNING] 1.x only. This page describes repo-guardian 1.x. v2 has no equivalent: chart 2.x is a fresh install, see Turning on repo-guardian v2.

[!NOTE] Superseded by chart 1.0.0-rc.1 (IMPL-0016). The memory/ticker defaults this runbook describes are no longer valid. The chart now ships Postgres + Valkey as the only supported backends. See migrations.md#removing-memory-backend for the current migration path. The 0.5.0 runbook is retained for historical context only.

Chart 0.5.0 ships IMPL-0011: durable Postgres-backed Store, Valkey-backed Queue with in-flight reaper, and SETNX leader-elected Scheduler — the multi-replica foundation.

(Historical) Defaults at the time of 0.5.0 release. store.backend=memory, queue.backend=memory, scheduler.backend=ticker. Operators upgrading from chart 0.3.x or 0.4.x at replicaCount: 1 got bit-identical behaviour with no values changes. Those backends were removed in chart 1.0.0-rc.1.

This runbook drives the upgrade in two stages so any regression is bisectable: no-op upgrade first, then multi-replica enablement.

docs.title: Pre-flight (5 min)
docs.text:
• [ ] Cosign-verify the chart artifact:

bash cosign verify \ --certificate-identity-regexp '^https://github.com/donaldgifford/repo-guardian/.+' \ --certificate-oidc-issuer 'https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com' \ ghcr.io/donaldgifford/charts/repo-guardian:0.5.0

  • [ ] Snapshot current cluster state (rollback baseline):

bash kubectl get deploy/repo-guardian -n repo-guardian -o yaml > /tmp/rg-pre-upgrade.yaml kubectl get pods -n repo-guardian

  • [ ] Read scaling.md and migrations.md for context on sizing knobs and Postgres schema lifecycle.

docs.title: Stage 1 — No-op upgrade to 0.5.0
docs.text:
Proves the chart-render upgrade path is clean. Defaults unchanged: store.backend=memory, queue.backend=memory, scheduler.backend=ticker, replicaCount: 1.

  • [ ] Bump the chart version in your ArgoCD Application (or kustomize helmCharts[0].version) from your current pin to 0.5.0. Do not change values yet.

  • [ ] helm template first and diff against current cluster state:

```bash helm template repo-guardian oci://ghcr.io/donaldgifford/charts/repo-guardian \ --version 0.5.0 \ -n repo-guardian \ -f your-values.yaml > /tmp/rg-0.5.0.yaml

diff <(kubectl get deploy/repo-guardian -n repo-guardian -o yaml) /tmp/rg-0.5.0.yaml | less ```

Expected diffs:

  • terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 60 (was 30)
  • New env vars: STORE_BACKEND=memory, QUEUE_BACKEND=memory, SCHEDULER_BACKEND=ticker, WORKER_CONCURRENCY=4, RECONCILE_FRESHNESS=7m, RATE_LIMIT_RESERVE=200

  • Image tag: 1.6.0

  • [ ] Apply (sync the ArgoCD app, or helm upgrade).

  • [ ] Verify pod restarts cleanly and image is correct:

bash kubectl rollout status deploy/repo-guardian -n repo-guardian kubectl get pod -n repo-guardian -o jsonpath='{.items[*].spec.containers[0].image}' # expect: ghcr.io/donaldgifford/repo-guardian:1.6.0

  • [ ] Smoke test — push a no-op commit to donaldgifford/logpush. Confirm webhook returns 202 and reconcile completes:

bash kubectl logs -n repo-guardian deploy/repo-guardian --tail=100 \ | grep -E 'webhook|reconcile|enqueue'

  • [ ] Bake for 24h. If anything misbehaves, roll the chart version pin back; defaults guarantee a clean rollback.

docs.title: Stage 2 — Enable multi-replica
docs.text:
The IMPL-0011 payoff. Pick the Postgres mode based on CNPG availability:

CNPG operator installed? Use this mode Yes cnpg (CNPG manages HA replicas, backups, monitoring) No baked (chart renders a single-pod Postgres StatefulSet)
  • [ ] Add the new values to your values file. Reference for cnpg + baked Valkey:

yaml replicaCount: 3 store: backend: postgres postgres: mode: cnpg # or "baked" if no CNPG queue: backend: valkey valkey: mode: baked scheduler: backend: valkey prometheusRule: enabled: true # 5 starter alerts

Reference for external (managed Postgres + Redis-compatible service) is documented in the chart README.

  • [ ] helm template again and diff. Expected new resources:

  • Cluster + optional Pooler (CNPG) OR StatefulSet / Service / Secret (baked Postgres)

  • StatefulSet / Service / Secret (Valkey)
  • PrometheusRule (5 alerts)

  • Deployment replicas: 3

  • [ ] Apply. Watch the bring-up:

bash kubectl get pods -n repo-guardian -w

Postgres comes up first; the repo-guardian deployment blocks on its readiness via the in-process migration runner. Expect 30-60s for the first pod to reach Ready.

docs.title: 1. Postgres schema applied
docs.text:
kubectl exec -n repo-guardian -it <postgres-pod> -- \
  psql -U repoguardian -d repoguardian -c '\dt'
# expect: repo_state, schema_migrations

docs.title: 2. Leader election holds
docs.text:
Exactly one of the three pods grabs the sweep lock per tick:

kubectl logs -n repo-guardian -l app.kubernetes.io/name=repo-guardian \
  --tail=200 --prefix | grep "scheduler tick acquired lock"
# expect: log lines from one pod only at any given moment

docs.title: 3. Webhook returns 202
docs.text:
Push a commit to donaldgifford/logpush:

kubectl logs -n repo-guardian -l app.kubernetes.io/name=repo-guardian \
  --tail=100 | grep "POST /webhook"
# expect: status=202

docs.title: 4. Reconcile completes & state row created
docs.text:
kubectl exec -n repo-guardian -it <postgres-pod> -- \
  psql -U repoguardian -d repoguardian \
  -c "SELECT installation_id, owner, repo, last_checked_at, last_check_status, policy_version
      FROM repo_state
      WHERE owner='donaldgifford' AND repo='logpush';"
# expect: one row, last_checked_at recent, last_check_status=success

docs.title: 5. Metrics endpoint exposes the new families
docs.text:
kubectl port-forward -n repo-guardian svc/repo-guardian 9090:9090 &
curl -s localhost:9090/metrics \
  | grep -E '^(queue_|scheduler_|store_query_seconds|rate_limit_)' \
  | head -20
# expect: queue_depth, queue_enqueued_total, scheduler_lock_acquired_total,
#         store_query_seconds_*, rate_limit_remaining

docs.title: 6. PrometheusRule loaded
docs.text:
(Skip if the Prometheus operator is not installed.)

kubectl get prometheusrule -n repo-guardian repo-guardian -o yaml \
  | grep -E '^\s+- alert:'
# expect 5 alerts: QueueDepthGrowing, QueueEnqueueErrors,
#                  SchedulerLeaderFlapping, StoreSlowQueries,
#                  RateLimitNearExhaustion

docs.title: 7. Leader failover within 30s
docs.text:
Kill the current leader; verify another pod picks up:

LEADER=$(kubectl logs -n repo-guardian -l app.kubernetes.io/name=repo-guardian \
  --tail=50 --prefix | grep "scheduler tick acquired lock" \
  | head -1 | awk -F'pod/' '{print $2}' | awk '{print $1}')

kubectl delete pod -n repo-guardian "$LEADER"
sleep 35

kubectl logs -n repo-guardian -l app.kubernetes.io/name=repo-guardian \
  --tail=50 --prefix | grep "scheduler tick acquired lock" | tail -3
# expect: lock acquired by a different pod within 30s

docs.title: 8. No duplicate reconciles
docs.text:
Wait through one full sweep cycle (default 7m) and check for duplicates:

kubectl logs -n repo-guardian -l app.kubernetes.io/name=repo-guardian \
  --tail=500 --prefix | grep "reconciled" | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -10
# expect: count of 1 per (owner/repo) per cycle, not 2-3

docs.title: Rollback
docs.text:
Fast rollback to single-replica. Flip values back to defaults; redeploy. The Postgres + Valkey StatefulSets/CRs stay in cluster (state preserved) but the binary stops using them:

replicaCount: 1
store: { backend: memory }
queue: { backend: memory }
scheduler: { backend: ticker }

Hard rollback to your previous chart version. Pin the chart version back; sync. The 0.5.0 backing resources (Postgres data, Valkey state) become orphaned but harmless — clean up later once you confirm the older chart is healthy:

kubectl delete sts,svc,secret -l app.kubernetes.io/instance=repo-guardian \
  -n repo-guardian

docs.title: Watch-list during the first 24h post-Stage-2
docs.text:
• queue_depth — should oscillate between 0 and ~N (your repo count) per sweep cycle, not climb monotonically.
  • scheduler_lock_acquired_total — should increment ~1× per tick (every 7m by default), only on the leader.
  • rate_limit_reserve_blocked_total — non-zero is fine if you have many installations; persistent climbing means lower STORE_SWEEP_BATCH_SIZE (or raise RATE_LIMIT_RESERVE).
  • repo_state.last_checked_at — for donaldgifford/logpush and donaldgifford/repo-guardian-test-repo, should refresh every ~7m.

docs.text:

  • DESIGN-0012 — design doc with the durable backend rationale (Postgres + Valkey, not NATS + embedded).
  • scaling.md — sizing knobs for replicaCount, workerCount, maxConns, staleSweep.*.
  • migrations.md — Postgres schema operations, out-of-band migration runs, backups, schema rollback.
  • Chart README — Choosing a deployment shape — the four shapes with use-case mapping.

docs.title: Homelab CNPG cutover runbook
docs.text:
[!NOTE] Superseded by chart 1.0.0-rc.1 (IMPL-0016). The memory → CNPG transition this runbook describes only applies to chart 0.6.x / 0.7.x operators. Chart 1.0.0-rc.1+ ships Postgres as the only supported store.backend, and the chart defaults already point at postgres.mode=cnpg if you set store.postgres.mode=cnpg. See migrations.md#removing-memory-backend for the post-IMPL-0016 migration path. This runbook is retained for operators still on chart 0.6.x / 0.7.x who want to cutover before bumping to 1.0.

You are running chart 0.6.x or 0.7.x with store.backend=memory (single-pod, no persistence) and want to switch to store.backend=postgres with postgres.mode=cnpg so reconcile state survives pod restarts.

This runbook assumes:

  • Chart 0.6.2 or newer (for the revisionHistoryLimit knob).
  • A Talos / vanilla k8s cluster managed via ArgoCD.
  • You're OK rotating the in-memory reconcile state — there's no migration from the memory store, you just lose the in-flight knowledge of which repos were recently swept (next sweep catches everything up).

For the full post-cutover smoke gate (8 checks: schema applied, leader-election working, queue draining, alerts firing, etc.), see chart-0.5.0-migration.md "Smoke checks". This doc focuses on the four homelab-specific gaps that runbook glosses over.

docs.title: 1. CNPG operator prerequisite
docs.text:
The chart renders a Cluster CR (postgresql.cnpg.io/v1) and an optional Pooler. Both require the CNPG operator to be installed before you apply the chart values change, or ArgoCD will sync the Application into a ComparisonError state.

# Verify the CRDs are present.
kubectl get crd | grep postgresql.cnpg.io
# Expected:
#   backups.postgresql.cnpg.io
#   clusters.postgresql.cnpg.io
#   poolers.postgresql.cnpg.io
#   scheduledbackups.postgresql.cnpg.io

If missing, install the operator first. The maintained path is the upstream Helm chart:

helm repo add cnpg https://cloudnative-pg.github.io/charts
helm upgrade --install cnpg cnpg/cloudnative-pg \
  --namespace cnpg-system \
  --create-namespace \
  --version 0.22.x

Pin to a known-good operator version (the chart was tested against CNPG operator 1.24.x lineage). The CNPG operator runs cluster-wide and only needs installing once per cluster.

docs.title: 2. Pick a StorageClass explicitly
docs.text:
The chart's store.postgres.cnpg.storage.storageClass defaults to "", which falls back to the cluster's default StorageClass. On Talos with multiple SCs (rook-ceph, local-path, longhorn, etc.) the "default" can drift silently — better to pin it.

kubectl get sc
# Pick the one you want; check it supports ReadWriteOnce.

Add to your values:

store:
  postgres:
    cnpg:
      storage:
        size: 10Gi
        storageClass: rook-ceph-block   # or whatever you picked

docs.title: 3. CNPG-created Secret timing
docs.text:
When mode=cnpg, the chart wires STORE_DSN from a Secret that the CNPG operator creates after it provisions the Cluster — typically named <release-name>-postgres-app, key uri. This secret does not exist at the moment ArgoCD applies the manifests; CNPG creates it during cluster bootstrap (10-60 seconds typical).

Consequence: the repo-guardian Deployment will CrashLoopBackOff during initial sync because its STORE_DSN env var references a Secret key that doesn't exist yet. This is expected and self-heals within 1-2 reconcile loops once CNPG finishes bootstrapping.

If you want the bring-up to look clean in ArgoCD's UI:

  • Add argocd.argoproj.io/sync-wave annotations so the CNPG Cluster resource lands before the Deployment. The chart doesn't ship these by default (they're cluster-policy-specific).
  • Or, use argocd.argoproj.io/sync-options: SkipDryRunOnMissingResource=true on the Application to suppress the noise.

For first-time bring-up, just let it CrashLoop for a minute and verify it recovers on its own.

docs.title: 4. revisionHistoryLimit (chart 0.6.2+)
docs.text:
You're already getting this — chart 0.6.2 defaults revisionHistoryLimit: 3. If you want a different value, set:

revisionHistoryLimit: 5

This applies to the repo-guardian Deployment only. The CNPG-managed Postgres Cluster has its own retention via the operator; not exposed through the repo-guardian chart.

docs.title: Values diff (homelab reference)
docs.text:
# Before (chart 0.6.x, memory store)
replicaCount: 1
store:
  backend: memory

# After (chart 0.6.2, CNPG store)
replicaCount: 1                         # bump to 3 if you also want HA
revisionHistoryLimit: 3                 # chart 0.6.2 default; explicit for clarity
store:
  backend: postgres
  postgres:
    mode: cnpg
    cnpg:
      instances: 1                      # bump to 3 for CNPG HA replicas
      storage:
        size: 10Gi
        storageClass: rook-ceph-block   # pin explicitly
      pooler:
        enabled: false                  # optional PgBouncer; skip for single-replica

If you also want to flip the queue + scheduler to durable backends in the same change (recommended for replicaCount > 1, optional for single-replica), add:

queue:
  backend: valkey
  valkey:
    mode: baked                         # single-pod Valkey from the chart
scheduler:
  backend: valkey                       # SETNX leader-election

The full multi-replica reference is in chart-0.5.0-migration.md Stage 2.

docs.title: Bring-up sequence
docs.text:
1. Cosign-verify the new chart version:

bash cosign verify \ --certificate-identity-regexp \ '^https://github.com/donaldgifford/repo-guardian/.+' \ --certificate-oidc-issuer \ 'https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com' \ ghcr.io/donaldgifford/charts/repo-guardian:0.6.2

  1. Render the chart locally and diff against the live state to confirm only expected resources change:

bash helm template repo-guardian \ oci://ghcr.io/donaldgifford/charts/repo-guardian \ --version 0.6.2 \ --namespace repo-guardian \ -f values.yaml > /tmp/rg-after.yaml diff <(kubectl get -n repo-guardian deploy,svc,sts,cluster.postgresql.cnpg.io \ -o yaml) /tmp/rg-after.yaml

Expect: new Cluster resource, new Service for Postgres, env var changes on the Deployment (STORE_BACKEND, STORE_DSN).

  1. Sync the ArgoCD Application or run helm upgrade.

  2. Watch the rollout:

bash kubectl get pods -n repo-guardian -w # Order: CNPG cluster pod(s) → repo-guardian (will crashloop briefly) # → repo-guardian Ready once Postgres is up.

  1. Once both pods are Ready, run the chart-0.5.0-migration.md smoke checks:

  2. Schema applied (\dt shows repo_state, schema_migrations)

  3. Pod restart no longer triggers a full re-sweep (the original reason for this cutover)
  4. store_query_seconds metric is populated
  5. No flapping in RepoGuardianStoreUnavailable alert

docs.title: Rollback
docs.text:
If something goes wrong, the rollback is values-only:

store:
  backend: memory

After applying, the chart drops the Cluster resource. The CNPG operator does not auto-delete the PVC; you'll need to do that by hand if you want the storage reclaimed:

kubectl delete pvc -n repo-guardian -l \
  cnpg.io/cluster=repo-guardian-postgres

The reconcile state in Postgres is lost on rollback (the memory store starts empty), but that's the same state you started with before this runbook.

docs.title: Optional: external access via the pooler LB Service (chart 0.7.0+)
docs.text:
When you need to reach the database from outside the cluster (psql shell from your laptop, a side-car backup tool, a connection from another cluster on the same BGP fabric), enable the pooler plus its LoadBalancer Service. Cilium does not currently support TCPRoute (cilium/cilium#42016), so the chart routes external connections through a regular Service: LoadBalancer and advertises the VIP via Cilium BGP labels.

store:
  postgres:
    cnpg:
      pooler:
        enabled: true                            # ← required for the LB Service
        instances: 2                             # 2 for HA, 1 for a homelab single-node
        type: rw
        pgbouncer:
          poolMode: transaction
        service:
          enabled: true
          type: LoadBalancer
          labels:
            bgp.cilium.io/advertise-service: default
            bgp.cilium.io/ip-pool: default

After upgrade, find the assigned VIP:

kubectl get svc -n repo-guardian \
  -l app.kubernetes.io/instance=repo-guardian \
  -o jsonpath='{range .items[?(@.spec.type=="LoadBalancer")]}{.metadata.name}{"\t"}{.status.loadBalancer.ingress[0].ip}{"\n"}{end}'

Connect with the credentials from the CNPG-managed <cluster>-app Secret (uri key is a ready-made DSN):

kubectl get secret repo-guardian-postgres-app -n repo-guardian \
  -o jsonpath='{.data.uri}' | base64 -d
# postgresql://<user>:<pw>@<cluster>:5432/<db>
# Swap <cluster> for the LB VIP from the previous command.

Both instances and the underlying CNPG Cluster.instances count should be ≥ 2 if external clients depend on this for production reads — a single-pooler-instance LB is a single restart away from dropping every external session.
