docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text:
A standard that nobody checks is a suggestion. Across hundreds of repositories and several organisations, the baseline everyone agrees on drifts as soon as it is written down:

  • Ownership. A repository with no CODEOWNERS has no required reviewer and no one to page. A repository with no catalog-info.yaml is missing from the service catalogue, so nobody can say who owns it, what it runs or which Jira project its bugs go to.
  • Supply chain. A repository without Dependabot or Renovate stops receiving dependency and security updates silently. One configured against the wrong preset receives the wrong ones. A repository with vulnerability alerts turned off does not tell anyone about a known CVE.
  • Change control. Without a branch ruleset, a single push can put unreviewed code on main, skip CI, or rewrite history.
  • Audit evidence. Frameworks such as SOC 2 and ISO 27001 ask for evidence that change control and dependency management are applied to every in-scope system, continuously. A spreadsheet assembled before the audit is out of date on the day it is finished.

repo-guardian turns the baseline into code, evaluates every repository against it continuously, and records the answer the business asks for: who is compliant with which control, since when, and why not. Where the policy says so, it also fixes what it finds.

docs.title: The short version
docs.text:
• Policy is a directory, not a file. enterprise.hcl names the organisations and the controls every repository gets, catalogue/ defines the controls, orgs/ adds per-org controls, exclusions and overrides, and templates/ overrides the embedded file templates. guardian.hcl is not read by v2.
  • The unit is a control. A control (codeowners@1) has a type, a version and a set of rules. Results, compliance and history are per control, and per rule inside it.
  • Two GitHub Apps. The Evaluation App reads. The Remediation App writes, and only to repositories you grant it.
  • Nothing is written until you say so. Every assignment evaluates; only one in mode = "remediate", on a repository the Remediation App can reach, opens pull requests or writes through the API.

docs.title: Controls and rules
docs.text:
A control is defined once in the catalogue and assigned by name and version:

# catalogue/codeowners.hcl
control "codeowners" {
  version     = 1
  type        = "codeowners"
  title       = "CODEOWNERS"
  description = "A CODEOWNERS file exists in one of GitHub's locations"
  template    = "codeowners"

  rule "exists" {
    title     = "A CODEOWNERS file exists"
    remediate = true
  }
}

# enterprise.hcl
enterprise {
  orgs     = ["myorg"]
  mode     = "evaluate"
  controls = ["codeowners@1"]
}

Each rule has a kind the control type declares (it defaults to the rule id when the id names a kind) and the parameters that kind takes. The control's status is derived from its rules' statuses, so a control with one failing rule is non-compliant and the result says which rule. remediate = true marks a rule repo-guardian may fix; a rule without it is reported only.

docs.title: The built-in control types
docs.text:
Type Checks Remediated by file one file exists, matches a template, or is absent pull request codeowners a CODEOWNERS file in one of GitHub's locations pull request catalog_info catalog-info.yaml is a Backstage Component with the fields you require and no placeholders pull request dependency_updates Renovate or Dependabot is configured, extends your preset, and is the only bot pull request repo_settings repository settings equal expected values API (apply) branch_ruleset a named repository ruleset exists and matches the declaration API (apply) labels labels are present with the right colour and description, or absent API (apply) custom_properties GitHub custom properties match catalog-info.yaml and the org schema API or a workflow PR (apply)

The parameters and rule kinds of each are in the control-type reference, which is generated from the types themselves and cannot drift from the code.

Why: these are the files and settings the rest of your tooling depends on. Review routing reads CODEOWNERS, update bots read their config, the service catalogue reads catalog-info.yaml, and org-wide rulesets, search and reporting select on custom properties. A missing or wrong one does not fail loudly; it quietly turns that tooling off for one repository.

docs.title: Who a control applies to
docs.text:
• enterprise.orgs lists every organisation repo-guardian manages. A repository in any other organisation is unmanaged: it is never evaluated and never counts.
  • enterprise.controls assigns controls to every managed repository. An org file's controls adds more for that org, and a repos "<name>" { match = [...] } block adds or replaces controls for a set of repositories.
  • exclude_repos and per-control exclude blocks take repositories or controls out of scope, and each requires a reason. An exclusion is recorded and reported with its reason; it is not a silent skip.
  • Archived and forked repositories are parked: not evaluated while they stay archived or forked, and their results cleared so they do not count.

docs.title: Evaluate and remediate
docs.text:
mode is set at the enterprise, org, repository-set or per-control level, and the most specific setting wins:

  • evaluate records results and changes nothing.
  • remediate also fixes remediate = true rules, but only where the Remediation App has access to the repository through an installation that is not suspended. Elsewhere the assignment runs as evaluate, with the reason (remediation_app_no_access or remediation_app_suspended) recorded on it and shown in the UI. That is not an error, and granting the App the repository lifts it without a policy edit.

API-remediated controls also choose how they write, with remediation { apply = ... } in the catalogue:

apply Does recommend (default) records the before and after values as a recommendation; writes nothing direct the remediator writes the change through the API, reads it back, and journals it per resource workflow a pull request adds .github/workflows/repo-guardian-<slug>.yml, which applies the change on merge (custom_properties only)

docs.title: How it fixes things
docs.text:
The remediator acts as the Remediation App, one run at a time per repository and control, and only for assignments in remediate mode.

  • One pull request per control. Each control that needs file changes gets its own branch, repo-guardian/<control slug>, and its own PR, updated in place as the results change. The branch carries no version, so a control version bump updates the same PR. A reviewer sees one concern per PR, and merging the Renovate PR never waits on the CODEOWNERS one.
  • Bounded noise. remediation { max_open_prs } (default 3) caps how many repo-guardian PRs a repository has open at once; the rest wait in policy order, held as pr_cap, and go out as PRs merge or close. reopen_after (default 14 days) is how long a PR a human closed stays closed while the control still fails; to stop it for good, exclude the control for that repository.
  • Humans win. A human may push to repo-guardian's PR. The remediator merges main into it, keeps human edits, reverts only its own obsolete changes, and never force-pushes. It adopts an existing branch only when the open PR on it was authored by the Remediation App's bot.
  • It closes what it opened. A PR is closed closed_compliant when a fresh read of main shows the control passing (a human's own fix, for instance), and closed_withdrawn when the control is no longer assigned, each with a comment. A merged PR is the end of that run.
  • Holds say why nothing happened. A control that cannot be remediated right now is held with a reason the UI and /remediations?hold= show:
Hold Means Clears when pr_cap the repository is at max_open_prs one of its PRs merges or closes foreign_branch repo-guardian/<slug> exists but its PR is not the App's the branch is removed or renamed stale_branch a branch is left from a PR a human closed without merging the branch is deleted conflict the PR's branch no longer descends from the App's last commit, or main will not merge cleanly a human resolves the branch permission the App may not make the change (for example a workflow file without the Workflows permission), or cannot reach the repository to clean up the App is granted the permission or the access
  • Branches are never deleted. Not after merge, not after a close, not to clear a hold. Branch cleanup after merge is the repository's delete_branch_on_merge setting, which a repo_settings control can enforce.
  • API controls follow apply. recommend writes nothing and records the change for a human; direct writes, reads back and journals each resource; workflow opens a PR with a workflow that applies it on merge. A recommendation ends superseded, withdrawn or resolved; it is never left dangling.

docs.title: Rolling out a new control safely
docs.text:
1. Add the control to the catalogue and assign it with mode = "evaluate" (a per-control override inside a remediate org works: control "name@1" { mode = "evaluate" }).
  2. Check it before deploying: repo-guardian evaluate --repo org/name --policy <root> evaluates one repository against the new policy with no database.
  3. Deploy and read the results: the UI, the API or repo-guardian report show how many repositories fail and on which rule.
  4. Add exclusions, each with its reason, for the legitimate exceptions.
  5. Switch the assignment to remediate and watch the first PRs, holds and the cap in the UI's Remediations view.

docs.title: Policy compatibility
docs.text: None at the file level: v2 does not read guardian.hcl, and there is no converter. Every concern v1 enforced has a control type, and the policy reference maps each v1 rule kind to its control. examples/policy/full is v1's guardian-full.hcl rewritten as a policy root, one control per concern.

docs.title: Rule kinds become control types
docs.text: v1 v2 rule "file" with check = "exists" file, or the typed control for that file (codeowners, catalog_info, dependency_updates) check = "contains" and assertion {} blocks the typed control's rules (catalog_info's field_set, dependency_updates's extends) check = "exact" file with an exact rule check = "absent" file with an absent rule; retiring Dependabot is dependency_updates's exclusive rule when { rule_satisfied } gates gone: a typed control checks the whole migration itself (exclusive passes only once Renovate is configured and Dependabot is gone) rule "setting" repo_settings, one rule per property rule "branch_protection" branch_ruleset, declared as the rulesets API body custom_properties reconciler custom_properties control (annotation_properties carries over) label_sync reconciler labels control branch_protection reconciler branch_ruleset control workflow_sync reconciler file with an exact rule on the workflow scope { orgs } enterprise.orgs plus per-org controls ignore { repos } exclude_repos and per-control exclude, each with a reason remediate = false on a rule mode = "evaluate", or a rule without remediate = true guardian { dry_run = true } mode = "evaluate"

docs.title: Pull requests
docs.text: v1 put every file change for a repository on one branch, repo-guardian/add-missing-files, under one PR. v2 opens one PR per control on repo-guardian/<slug>, capped by max_open_prs. Because the branch names differ, v2 does not adopt v1's open PRs: close them per org with rgctl once that org turns on remediate (cutover step 6). PR title, body and labels are still templated, now per control with pr {} in the catalogue.

docs.title: What was dropped
docs.text:
• search_terms and foreign-PR detection. v1 left a rule alone when it found someone else's PR that looked like it addressed the rule. That guess made a repository read as compliant while nothing was merged. v2 reports the repository's actual state; a human PR that fixes it turns the control compliant when it merges.
  • The sticky reconcile-log comment. The UI's per-repository event history replaces it.
  • Auto-close and orphan cleanup knobs. One PR per control makes them part of the model instead of options.

docs.title: Names that changed
docs.text: v1 / v2 rc Controls line CHECK_INTERVAL EVAL_INTERVAL GUARDIAN_CONFIG = a file GUARDIAN_CONFIG = the policy root directory worker role evaluator and remediator roles, one per App RepoWorkflow (repo/<id>) EvaluationWorkflow (evaluation/<id>) DiscoveryWorkflow, discovery schedule ControlsDiscoveryWorkflow, controls-discovery schedule SnapshotWorkflow, snapshot schedule ControlsSnapshotWorkflow, controls-snapshot schedule policy-rollout/<v> controls-rollout/<version>/<activated at> findings, /findings, /rules results, /repositories/{id}/controls, /controls

docs.title: The status model
docs.text:
Every rule result is compliant, non_compliant, not_applicable or unknown, with a reason and typed evidence. A control's status follows from its rules.

Compliance is reported over assignments (repository × control), and every assignment lands in exactly one bucket:

Bucket Means compliant, non_compliant measured not_applicable measured, the control does not apply (for example, a catalog-info.yaml that is not a Component) unknown evaluated, but the input could not be judged (a parse error, an inherited ruleset) pending assigned, no result yet stale the result is from an older assignment or control revision unmeasurable_access_denied, unmeasurable_suspended the Evaluation App cannot read the repository unmeasurable_conflict two assigned controls own the same resource; an operator must fix the policy excluded excluded by policy, with a reason

Two numbers come out of that. Percent is compliant over compliant plus non-compliant. Coverage is measured (compliant, non-compliant, not applicable) over assigned. Both are floored to one decimal in SQL, and both are no data, never 100%, on an empty denominator: nothing measured is not a perfect fleet.

docs.title: Where v2 is a real improvement
Compliance you can trust
docs.text:
v1 records one boolean per repository and rule, and everything that is not actionable reads as compliant, including an open foreign PR, a missing branch, an unreadable repository and a rule nobody evaluated.

v2 gives every control result a status, a reason, rule-level detail and evidence, keeps an append-only event history per result, and reports what it could not measure as its own bucket instead of folding it into "compliant". The percentage is computed by one SQL function shared by the report, the API, the UI and the daily snapshots.

docs.title: A durable control plane instead of a hand-rolled one
docs.text:
v1 runs its own job system on Valkey (a list, two sorted sets, a reaper and SETNX leader election), with every invariant in hand-written Lua.

v2 hands that to Temporal. Each repository is a long-lived EvaluationWorkflow that schedules its own next evaluation, coalesces the signals that arrive meanwhile (a push, a policy change, a re-evaluate button press), and survives pod restarts. Schedules need no leader, and Valkey is gone.

docs.title: One rate budget per installation, per App
docs.text: An InstallationWorkflow per installation and App holds its budget: remaining calls, the reset time, outstanding leases and a moving estimate of what an evaluation costs. An evaluation acquires a lease before it spends. Webhook-triggered work sees half the reserve, so a human-triggered evaluation jumps the queue during a fleet-wide one. The Evaluation App's reads can never starve the Remediation App's writes, because they are separate budgets.

docs.title: Cosmetic edits re-evaluate nothing
docs.text: A control's identity for results is its revision: a digest over its type, version, rules and parameters, apply, its template and the files it references, but not its title, description or PR text. Editing a template or a rule re-evaluates the repositories assigned that control. Fixing a typo in a title re-evaluates nothing. Operational knobs are environment variables and never part of the policy version.

docs.title: Policy changes roll out, they do not stampede
docs.text: A newly activated policy version starts one controls-rollout workflow, which spreads every affected repository's next evaluation across the rollout window. A revert to an earlier version rolls out again, because each activation is its own rollout. Results from an assignment that changed mid-evaluation are fenced off by the assignment's epoch and discarded rather than written over the new one.

docs.title: Least privilege by App and by role
docs.text:
• Two Apps. The Evaluation App has read permissions only. The Remediation App writes, and is installed only where you want writes.
  • ingest receives webhooks for both Apps on separate routes, holds only the webhook secrets, and refuses to start with an App key or a database DSN.
  • evaluator holds the Evaluation App key and a database role that can write results but nothing remediation-related.
  • remediator holds the Remediation App key and its own database role. It scales to zero independently.
  • api reads through a read-only database role. Its one write is sending a re-evaluate signal.

The chart mounts each key and DSN only into the role that needs it, and a helm-unittest suite asserts every absence.

docs.title: Webhooks that fail loudly and deduplicate
docs.text: Ingest starts a workflow keyed on X-GitHub-Delivery, so a redelivery is a no-op success. If Temporal cannot accept the event, ingest answers 503 and GitHub records the delivery as failed and redeliverable. Events nothing acts on get a 204 before any work is scheduled, and a push re-evaluates only the controls that own or read a path it changed.

docs.title: Repositories keep their identity across renames and transfers
docs.text: Repositories are matched on GitHub's repository ID first. A rename or transfer keeps the same row, results, history and workflow, and records a renamed or transferred event. A name now held by a different repository ID is refused as a conflict rather than guessed at.

docs.title: Parking that never guesses
docs.text: Archived and forked repositories, and repositories the Evaluation App lost, are parked. Discovery parks a repository as removed only after a complete listing of its installation, so a failed or partial listing parks nothing. Parks that mean "we know nothing applies" (archived, fork, removed) clear the repository's results; parks that mean "we could not read it" (access denied) keep them, so a transient 403 never makes a repository look compliant.

docs.title: Answers for people who do not read PromQL
docs.text:
• A read-only REST API (OpenAPI 3.1, OIDC, per-org authorization) over controls, organisations, repositories, results, events, history and the active policy. See the API.
  • A web UI: fleet posture, per-control and per-org drill-downs, each repository's controls with rule detail and evidence, compliance history, and the active policy. See the business UI.
  • A public status page, privacy-checked by a test so it cannot leak a repository or org name.

Generated Grafana dashboards and alerts are derived from the policy (repo-guardian monitoring generate --config <root>), keyed on control.

docs.title: Safe rollouts of the service itself
docs.text: The evaluator and remediator each run their own Temporal worker deployment. A worker promotes its build only when it is newer by semver, so a crash-looping pod of the previous release cannot pull a rollout backwards, and a remediator at zero replicas never blocks the evaluator. Workflow code is replay-tested against captured histories in CI.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: v1 v2 (controls) Policy one guardian.hcl a policy directory: enterprise, catalogue, orgs, templates Unit rule, actionable boolean control with rules: status, reason, evidence, history Unmeasured reads as compliant its own bucket; coverage reported beside percent GitHub access one App, reads and writes Evaluation App reads, Remediation App writes Pull requests one branch per repository one branch per control, capped by max_open_prs Job system Valkey queue, reaper, Lua, SETNX leader Temporal workflows and schedules Rate limiting reactive defer per-installation, per-App budget with leases and priorities Cosmetic policy edit re-checks the fleet changes nothing Policy change every repository stale at once rolled out over a window, fenced by epoch Webhook failure 202 anyway; lost 503, redeliverable, deduplicated Rename or transfer new repository same repository, event recorded Consumers Prometheus and logs API, UI, status page, report, plus Prometheus

docs.title: Verifying releases
docs.text:
Every repo-guardian artefact is signed and carries provenance you can check before you run it:

Artefact Where Signed with Provenance SBOM Image ghcr.io/donaldgifford/repo-guardian cosign keyless SLSA Level 3 (slsa-github-generator) SPDX, cosign attestation UI image ghcr.io/donaldgifford/repo-guardian-ui cosign keyless SLSA Level 3 SPDX, cosign attestation Chart oci://ghcr.io/donaldgifford/charts/repo-guardian cosign keyless SLSA Level 3 SPDX, cosign attestation Binaries GitHub release assets GPG over checksums.txt none yet SPDX *.sbom.json beside each archive

Images are tagged without the v (2.0.0), git tags and releases with it (v2.0.0). The ECR mirror, where enabled, carries the same signatures under its own registry path.

  • What you need
  • The signing identity
  • Signatures
  • SLSA provenance
  • SBOMs
  • Binaries

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• cosign v2 or v3.
  • slsa-verifier for the alternative provenance check.
  • gpg and sha256sum (or shasum -a 256) for the binaries.

Verify by digest where you can: a tag can be moved, a digest cannot. docker buildx imagetools inspect <image>:<tag> prints it.

docs.title: The signing identity
docs.text:
The images and the chart are signed and their SBOMs attested by the publish workflows through GitHub's OIDC token, so the certificate's identity is the workflow file and the ref it ran from:

  • a release from main runs ghcr.yml as a reusable workflow of release.yml, so the identity is https://github.com/donaldgifford/repo-guardian/.github/workflows/ghcr.yml@refs/heads/main;
  • a hand-published release candidate runs ghcr.yml from its tag: https://github.com/donaldgifford/repo-guardian/.github/workflows/ghcr.yml@refs/tags/v2.0.0-rc.18.

The commands below match either with one expression. Pin the exact identity instead when you know how the version was published. The issuer is always https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com.

ID='^https://github\.com/donaldgifford/repo-guardian/\.github/workflows/(ghcr|ecr)\.yml@refs/(heads/main|tags/v.+)$'
ISSUER='https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com'

docs.title: Signatures
docs.text:
cosign verify --certificate-identity-regexp "$ID" --certificate-oidc-issuer "$ISSUER" \
  ghcr.io/donaldgifford/repo-guardian:2.0.0

cosign verify --certificate-identity-regexp "$ID" --certificate-oidc-issuer "$ISSUER" \
  ghcr.io/donaldgifford/repo-guardian-ui:2.0.0

cosign verify --certificate-identity-regexp "$ID" --certificate-oidc-issuer "$ISSUER" \
  ghcr.io/donaldgifford/charts/repo-guardian:2.0.0

A pass prints the verified payload as JSON. Any other identity, or none, is a failure.

docs.title: SLSA provenance
docs.text:
Provenance is written by the SLSA GitHub generator, so its identity is the generator's workflow, not ours:

cosign verify-attestation --type slsaprovenance \
  --new-bundle-format=false \
  --certificate-identity-regexp '^https://github\.com/slsa-framework/slsa-github-generator/.+' \
  --certificate-oidc-issuer "$ISSUER" \
  ghcr.io/donaldgifford/repo-guardian:2.0.0

Swap the reference for the UI image or the chart. --new-bundle-format=false is needed on cosign v3: it reads only new-bundle referrers by default, the generator writes the legacy .att tag, and without the flag cosign reports a misleading identity mismatch against our own signature.

slsa-verifier checks the same provenance against the source repository and tag:

slsa-verifier verify-image \
  ghcr.io/donaldgifford/repo-guardian@sha256:<digest> \
  --source-uri github.com/donaldgifford/repo-guardian \
  --source-tag v2.0.0

The provenance records the workflow, the source commit and the builder, which is what an admission policy can enforce.

docs.title: SBOMs
docs.text:
Each image and the chart carries an SPDX SBOM as a cosign attestation, generated by syft over the published digest:

cosign verify-attestation --type spdxjson \
  --certificate-identity-regexp "$ID" --certificate-oidc-issuer "$ISSUER" \
  ghcr.io/donaldgifford/repo-guardian:2.0.0 > /dev/null

To read it (cosign v3 writes a sigstore bundle, so the in-toto statement is the bundle's DSSE payload):

cosign download attestation --predicate-type https://spdx.dev/Document \
  ghcr.io/donaldgifford/repo-guardian:2.0.0 \
  | jq -r '.dsseEnvelope.payload' | base64 -d | jq '.predicate'

The images' buildkit attestations (docker buildx imagetools inspect --format '{{ json .SBOM }}') carry a second SBOM from the build itself; the cosign attestation is the one signed by our identity.

docs.title: Binaries
docs.text:
Each GitHub release has the archives, an SPDX SBOM per archive (*.sbom.json), checksums.txt covering both, and checksums.txt.sig, a detached GPG signature by the release key:

C47D 59D8 6FC2 4BAE C5BB  3271 2E2C EA0B C2BD 8D59

gpg --verify checksums.txt.sig checksums.txt
sha256sum --ignore-missing -c checksums.txt

Check that gpg reports a good signature from that fingerprint, then that every file you downloaded is OK. IMPL-0036 replaces the GPG signature with cosign and SLSA provenance for the binaries, like the images.

docs.title: Plans
docs.text: Planning documents that capture the goal, approach, and component breakdown for a piece of work. Plans sit between a design document (what) and an implementation plan (how step-by-step). Use a plan when the scope is clear but the execution approach needs to be worked out before writing tasks.

docs.title: repo-guardian 2.0.0
docs.text: [!IMPORTANT] 2.0.0 is a fresh install, and latest now points at it. It does not read a 1.x guardian.hcl, the 2.x chart refuses every 1.x value at render time, and the database schema is new. Anyone pulling ghcr.io/donaldgifford/repo-guardian:latest gets 2.0.0 from this release on: pin 1.14.1 to stay on 1.x. The chart defaults its image tag to its appVersion, so chart users are unaffected unless they set image.tag: latest.

docs.title: What 2.0 is
docs.text:
repo-guardian evaluates every repository in your GitHub organisations against a policy you keep as code, records who is compliant with which control and why not, and, where the policy says so, fixes it.

  • Controls, not rules. The policy is a directory: enterprise.hcl names the organisations and the baseline, catalogue/ defines versioned controls (codeowners@1), orgs/ adds per-org controls, exclusions and overrides, templates/ overrides the embedded files. Eight built-in control types cover files and the GitHub API. See the policy reference and the control-type reference.
  • Two GitHub Apps. The Evaluation App reads everything; the Remediation App writes, only where you install it. Each is held by its own role, with its own key.
  • Remediation you opt into. Only an assignment in mode = "remediate" writes: one pull request per control on a repo-guardian/<control> branch, or a direct API change. It never force-pushes and never deletes a branch.
  • Temporal and Postgres. Every repository has its own durable evaluation workflow, with a rate budget per installation per App. Results and their history live in Postgres behind per-role database users that can each write only their own columns.
  • A business UI and a read-only API. Compliance by control and org, findings with their evidence, remediations and holds, and history, without PromQL, behind your identity provider.

docs.title: Installing
docs.text:
Follow Getting started, then Turning on repo-guardian v2:

helm install repo-guardian oci://ghcr.io/donaldgifford/charts/repo-guardian \
  --version 2.0.0 --namespace repo-guardian --create-namespace -f values.yaml

Moving from 1.x: Migrating from v1 to v2 lists every removed variable and value with its replacement, and rgctl finds and closes the pull requests 1.x opened.

docs.title: Identity providers
docs.text: The API and UI work with Keycloak, Okta, Entra ID and Auth0 without code changes; Identity providers has a recipe and a sign-in check for each.

docs.title: Verifying this release
docs.text: The images, the UI image and the chart are signed with cosign (keyless) and carry SLSA Level 3 provenance and an SPDX SBOM attestation; the binaries ship an SPDX SBOM per archive and a GPG-signed checksums.txt. The commands are in Verifying releases.

docs.title: Supported versions
docs.text: 2.x is supported. 1.14.x receives security fixes for 90 days after 2.0.0; see SECURITY.md.

docs.title: Requests for Comments (RFCs)
docs.text: This directory contains RFCs documenting high-level proposals for major features and system redesigns.

docs.title: What are RFCs?
docs.text:
RFCs document high-level problem definitions and solution strategies. Each RFC focuses on:

  • Problem Statement: The issue being addressed with evidence
  • Proposed Solution: High-level approach and architecture
  • Implementation Phases: Overview of how the solution will be built
  • Alternatives: Other approaches that were considered
  • Risks and Success Criteria: What could go wrong and how we measure success

docs.title: Creating a New RFC
docs.text: docz create rfc "Your RFC Title"

docs.title: RFC Status
docs.text:
• Draft: Initial draft, not yet ready for review
  • Proposed: Ready for review and feedback
  • Accepted: Approved and ready for implementation
  • Rejected: Not moving forward with this proposal
  • Superseded: Replaced by another RFC

docs.title: RFC 0001: Repo Compliance App (repo-guardian)
docs.text: Status: Draft Author: Donald Gifford Date: 2026-02-06

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Automated GitHub App that detects missing configuration files (CODEOWNERS, Dependabot, Renovate) across a GitHub organization and creates pull requests with sensible defaults. Deployed to Kubernetes (EKS) with webhook-driven and scheduled reconciliation.

docs.title: Problem Statement
docs.text:
Across a large GitHub organization with hundreds (or thousands) of repositories, there is no automated enforcement ensuring that newly created or onboarded repositories contain baseline configuration files such as CODEOWNERS, Dependabot configuration, and Renovate configuration. Engineers frequently create repos and forget to add these files, leading to inconsistent dependency management, unclear ownership, and compliance drift.

Manual enforcement does not scale. We need an automated system that detects missing files and creates pull requests to add sensible defaults, while being easily extensible to enforce additional files in the future.

docs.title: Goals
docs.text:
1. Automatically detect when a repository is created or newly added (i.e., the app is installed on a repo it hasn't processed before) within a GitHub org or set of repos.
  2. Run a scheduled weekly reconciliation across all installed repositories.
  3. For each repo, check for the existence of a configurable set of required files.
  4. If a file is missing, check whether an open PR already exists to add it before taking action.
  5. If no file and no open PR exist, create a branch with the missing file(s) and open a PR.
  6. Design the file-check system to be easily extensible -- adding a new required file should require minimal code changes.

docs.title: Non-Goals
docs.text:
• Enforcing file content beyond providing sensible defaults (no linting/validation of existing files).
  • Blocking merges or acting as a required status check (this is additive, not gatekeeping).
  • Managing GitHub App installation lifecycle (admins install manually; the app reacts).
  • Multi-GitHub-Enterprise support (single GitHub instance target, extendable later).

docs.title: Proposed Solution
docs.text: A Go-based GitHub App deployed to EKS that combines webhook-driven reactions with scheduled reconciliation. The core design centers on a pluggable FileRule registry where each rule defines what file to check, where to look for it, and what default template to use.

docs.title: Components
docs.text: Component Responsibility Webhook Handler Receives GitHub webhook events (installation_repositories, repository), validates signatures, enqueues repo checks. Scheduler Triggers a full reconciliation of all installed repos on a weekly cadence. Implemented as either an in-process ticker or a Kubernetes CronJob that hits an internal endpoint. Checker Engine Core logic: given a repo, iterate through the file rule registry, check for existence, check for open PRs, and create branches/PRs for missing files. File Rule Registry A pluggable list of "rules" -- each rule defines what file(s) to look for, alternate paths, and a default template. Adding a new rule = adding a new struct instance. GitHub API Client Thin wrapper around google/go-github for repo contents, branches, commits, and PRs. Uses GitHub App installation tokens.

docs.title: Authentication
docs.text:
The app uses the standard GitHub App authentication flow (not OAuth user tokens):

  1. App-level JWT: Signed with the app's RSA private key, used to list installations and generate installation tokens.
  2. Installation Access Token: Short-lived token scoped to the specific org/repos where the app is installed. Used for all API operations (reading files, creating branches, opening PRs).

docs.title: Required Permissions
docs.text: Permission Access Reason Contents Read & Write Read repo files, create branches, push commits Pull Requests Read & Write Check for open PRs, create new PRs Metadata Read Required for all apps, list repos

docs.title: Webhook Events
docs.text: Event Trigger repository (action: created) A new repo is created in the org installation_repositories (action: added) Repos are added to an existing app installation installation (action: created) App is newly installed on an org/repos

docs.title: File Rule Registry (Extensibility Core)
docs.text:
The central design principle: every file we want to enforce is represented as a FileRule. Adding a new file means adding a new rule to the registry -- no other code changes required.

type FileRule struct {
    Name                string
    Paths               []string
    PRSearchTerms       []string
    DefaultTemplateName string
    TargetPath          string
    Enabled             bool
}

Initial rule set: CODEOWNERS, Dependabot, Renovate.

docs.title: Checker Engine Flow
docs.text:
For each repo processed (whether triggered by webhook or scheduler):

  1. Get installation token.
  2. Iterate FileRule list. For each enabled rule:
  3. Check if any Path exists in repo. If found, skip rule.
  4. Search open PRs for PRSearchTerms. If found, skip rule.
  5. Otherwise, add to "missing" list.
  6. If any missing files: create single branch (repo-guardian/add-missing-files), commit all missing default files in one commit, create PR with summary.

Key design decisions:

  • All missing files bundled into a single branch and single PR.
  • Deterministic branch name for idempotent PR creation.
  • If the app's own PR branch already exists and is open, it updates the existing PR by force-pushing.

docs.title: Webhook Handler
docs.text: Handles three event types: RepositoryEvent (created), InstallationRepositoriesEvent (added), InstallationEvent (created). Each enqueues repos to the work queue.

docs.title: Scheduler
docs.text: In-process ticker (Option A from RFC). Runs reconcileAll on startup and at configured interval (default 168h / 1 week). Lists all installations, all repos, and enqueues each.

docs.title: Work Queue
docs.text: Buffered channel with configurable worker count. Workers pull jobs and call the Checker Engine. Provides concurrency control and backpressure against GitHub API rate limits.

docs.title: Template Management
docs.text: Default file contents stored in a Kubernetes ConfigMap mounted into the pod. Templates loaded at startup with embedded fallbacks.

docs.title: Kubernetes Deployment
docs.text: Single replica deployment with resource limits, liveness/readiness probes, volume mounts for private key and templates. Service exposes ports 80->8080 and 9090->9090. ALB Ingress Controller for webhook endpoint.

docs.title: PR Behavior
docs.text: Scenario Behavior All files exist No action Files missing, no open PR Create branch + PR Files missing, app's own PR already open Update existing PR (force-push branch) Files missing, someone else's PR addresses it No action (detected via PR search) Repo is archived Skip entirely Repo is a fork Skip (configurable) Empty repo (no default branch) Skip, log warning

docs.title: Observability
docs.text: 8 Prometheus metrics: repos checked, PRs created/updated, files missing, check duration, webhooks received, errors, GitHub rate limit remaining. Structured JSON logging via slog.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text: All configuration via environment variables (12-factor): GITHUB_APP_ID, GITHUB_PRIVATE_KEY_PATH, GITHUB_WEBHOOK_SECRET, LISTEN_ADDR, METRICS_ADDR, WORKER_COUNT, QUEUE_SIZE, TEMPLATE_DIR, SCHEDULE_INTERVAL, SKIP_FORKS, SKIP_ARCHIVED, DRY_RUN, LOG_LEVEL.

docs.title: Security
docs.text:
1. Webhook signature validation via github.ValidatePayload().
  2. Least-privilege permissions (Contents R/W, Pull Requests R/W, Metadata R).
  3. Secret management via Kubernetes Secrets (optionally backed by AWS Secrets Manager).
  4. Installation token scope limited to installed repos.
  5. Network policy restricts egress to GitHub API, ingress to ALB + GitHub webhook IPs.

docs.title: Alternatives Considered
docs.text:
• Kubernetes CronJob for scheduling instead of in-process ticker. More observability but more moving parts. Starting with in-process ticker for simplicity.
  • Per-file PRs instead of bundling all missing files into one PR. Rejected to avoid notification noise.
  • Status checks / merge blocking instead of additive PRs. Rejected as this should be additive, not gatekeeping.

docs.title: Phase 1: Foundation (Week 1-2)
docs.text:
• Register GitHub App, scaffold Go project.
  • Implement GitHub client wrapper, FileRule registry, Checker Engine.

docs.title: Phase 2: Webhook + Scheduler (Week 3)
docs.text: • Webhook handler, scheduler, work queue, observability.

docs.title: Phase 3: Deployment (Week 4)
docs.text: • Docker image, EKS deployment, ALB Ingress, dry-run validation.

docs.title: Phase 4: Production (Week 5)
docs.text: • Production rollout, monitoring, disable dry-run.

docs.title: Phase 5: Extend (Ongoing)
docs.text: • Additional FileRule entries, ConfigMap-driven rules, Slack notifications.

docs.title: Risks and Mitigations
docs.text: Risk Impact Likelihood Mitigation GitHub API rate limiting during large reconciliation High Medium Work queue with configurable concurrency, rate limit transport middleware Duplicate PRs from race conditions Medium Low Deterministic branch naming, idempotent PR creation Template content not suitable for all repos Low High PRs require human review, sensible defaults as starting point App credentials compromised High Low K8s Secrets, least-privilege permissions, IRSA for AWS

docs.title: Success Criteria
docs.text:
• All new repositories automatically receive PRs for missing configuration files within the webhook delivery window.
  • Weekly reconciliation catches any repos that were missed or had files removed.
  • Adding a new required file takes < 30 minutes of developer time (new FileRule + template).
  • Zero duplicate PRs created across webhook and scheduler triggers.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• GitHub Apps Documentation
  • go-github v68
  • ghinstallation v2
  • Kustomize

docs.title: RFC 0002: HCL-driven Policy Engine for repo-guardian
docs.text: Status: Accepted Author: Donald Gifford Date: 2026-03-14

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Replace repo-guardian's hardcoded file rules, special-cased custom properties checker, and environment-variable-only configuration with a unified HCL-driven policy engine. Rules, reconcilers, ignore lists, and org-level settings are all declared in a configuration file, making it possible to add new compliance checks, file-change-triggered reconciliation, and per-repo overrides without code changes.

docs.title: Problem Statement
docs.text:
repo-guardian currently has two separate code paths that are conceptually the same thing at different maturity levels:

  1. File rules (CODEOWNERS, dependabot, renovate) -- hardcoded Go structs in internal/rules/registry.go. Adding a new rule means writing Go code, recompiling, and redeploying. Rules are binary: the file exists or it doesn't. There is no post-merge reconciliation.

  2. Custom properties checker (internal/checker/properties.go) -- a completely separate code path that also checks for a file (catalog-info.yaml), but additionally reads the file's contents and reconciles derived state (GitHub custom properties). This is special-cased rather than being a capability any rule can have.

Both follow the same pattern: ensure a file exists in a repo; if not, PR it; optionally, when the file exists, read it and reconcile something.

Additional pain points:

  • No ignore/exclusion mechanism. There is no way to say "skip this rule for these repos" or "ignore this repo entirely" without code changes. At scale (10k+ repos), there will always be exceptions.

  • No push-event feedback loop. When repo-guardian creates a PR to add catalog-info.yaml and the PR is merged, the app has no way to detect the change until the next scheduler cycle (default 168h). This is because the app doesn't subscribe to push events.

  • Env vars don't scale. Configuration is entirely via environment variables. This works for a handful of settings but breaks down for structured data like rule definitions, per-repo overrides, field mappings, and multi-org support. You cannot express "for repos matching org/infra-*, skip the renovate rule" in an env var.

  • No content validation. Rules only check if a file exists. There is no way to verify a file's contents are correct -- e.g., CODEOWNERS has an actual owner (not a placeholder), or dependabot.yml includes the github-actions ecosystem.

  • No multi-org support path. The current architecture assumes a single GitHub org. As the tool grows, it needs a way to scope rules and configuration per-org.

docs.title: Proposed Solution
docs.text:
Introduce an HCL configuration file (guardian.hcl) that declaratively defines:

  • Rules -- typed compliance checks (file presence, content validation, repo settings, branch protection)
  • Reconcilers -- optional post-change behaviors attached to rules (e.g., read a file and sync derived state somewhere)
  • Ignore lists -- repos to skip globally or per-rule, with glob support
  • Push event handling -- which file changes trigger re-evaluation
  • Operational settings -- worker count, queue size, schedule interval, dry-run, etc. (with env var overrides)

docs.title: Why HCL
docs.text:
Feature HCL YAML Env Vars Typed blocks Yes No (flat maps) No Expressions/functions Yes No No Comments Yes Yes No References between blocks Yes No No Conditionals Yes No No Validation DSL Via hcldec External Manual Familiarity Terraform users Universal Universal Nested structure Natural Indentation-based Flat

HCL is chosen over YAML because it provides typed blocks, expressions, references between blocks, and composition primitives that map naturally to policy configuration. It's the same format the team uses with Terraform, so the learning curve is zero.

docs.title: Configuration File: guardian.hcl
docs.text:
# Operational settings -- all have built-in defaults, all can be
# overridden by environment variables.
guardian {
  dry_run            = false
  schedule_interval  = "168h"
  worker_count       = 5
  queue_size         = 1000
  log_level          = "info"
}

# Global ignore list -- these repos are skipped for ALL rules.
ignore {
  repos = [
    "myorg/legacy-monolith",
    "myorg/archived-*",
    "myorg/terraform-*",
  ]
}

# --- File presence and content rules ---

rule "file" "codeowners" {
  check  = "contains"   # exists | contains | exact
  paths  = [".github/CODEOWNERS", "CODEOWNERS", "docs/CODEOWNERS"]
  target = ".github/CODEOWNERS"
  template = "codeowners.tmpl"

  assertion {
    pattern = "^[^#].*@"
    message = "CODEOWNERS must contain at least one owner"
  }

  assertion {
    not_pattern = "@org/CHANGEME"
    message     = "CODEOWNERS still contains the placeholder team"
  }

  pr {
    search_terms = ["codeowners", "CODEOWNERS"]
  }

  ignore {
    repos = ["myorg/special-case"]
  }
}

rule "file" "dependabot" {
  check    = "contains"
  paths    = [".github/dependabot.yml", ".github/dependabot.yaml"]
  target   = ".github/dependabot.yml"
  template = "dependabot.tmpl"

  assertion {
    yaml_path = "updates[*].package-ecosystem"
    contains  = "github-actions"
    message   = "dependabot must include github-actions ecosystem"
  }

  pr {
    search_terms = ["dependabot"]
  }
}

rule "file" "renovate" {
  enabled = false

  check = "exists"
  paths = [
    "renovate.json",
    "renovate.json5",
    ".renovaterc",
    ".renovaterc.json",
    ".github/renovate.json",
    ".github/renovate.json5",
  ]
  target   = "renovate.json"
  template = "renovate.tmpl"

  pr {
    search_terms = ["renovate"]
  }
}

rule "file" "catalog_info" {
  check    = "exists"
  paths    = ["catalog-info.yaml", "catalog-info.yml"]
  target   = "catalog-info.yaml"
  template = "catalog-info.tmpl"

  pr {
    search_terms = ["catalog-info"]
  }

  # When the file exists or is modified, reconcile custom properties
  reconcile "custom_properties" {
    mode  = "api"   # or "github-action"
    watch = true    # trigger on push events

    owner       = "spec.owner"
    component   = "metadata.name"
    jira_project = "metadata.annotations.jira/project-key"
    jira_label   = "metadata.annotations.jira/label"

    defaults {
      owner     = "Unclassified"
      component = "Unclassified"
    }
  }
}

rule "file" "ci_lint" {
  check    = "exact"
  paths    = [".github/workflows/lint.yml"]
  target   = ".github/workflows/lint.yml"
  template = "lint-workflow.tmpl"

  pr {
    search_terms = ["lint workflow"]
  }

  reconcile "workflow_sync" {
    watch = true
  }
}

# --- Repository setting rules ---

rule "setting" "vulnerability_alerts" {
  property  = "vulnerability_alerts_enabled"
  expected  = true
  remediate = true
}

rule "setting" "default_branch" {
  property = "default_branch"
  expected = "main"
}

# --- Branch protection rules ---

rule "branch_protection" "main" {
  branch                = "main"
  require_pr            = true
  required_approvals    = 1
  dismiss_stale_reviews = true
  require_status_checks = ["ci/lint", "ci/test"]

  reconcile "branch_protection" {
    watch = true
  }
}

docs.title: Config File Loading
docs.text:
Supports both single file and directory loading. The GUARDIAN_CONFIG env var (default: /etc/repo-guardian/guardian.hcl) can point to either:

  • A single .hcl file
  • A directory containing one or more .hcl files

When pointing to a directory, all .hcl files are loaded and merged. HCL handles block merging natively. This allows splitting large configurations into logical files (e.g., rules-files.hcl, rules-settings.hcl, ignores.hcl).

docs.title: Architecture Overview
docs.text:
guardian.hcl (file or directory)
    |
    v
+-------------------+
| HCL Config Loader |  (internal/policy)
| - Parse & validate|
| - Build rule set  |
| - Merge env vars  |
+-------------------+
    |
    v
+-------------------+     +-------------------+
| Rule Engine       |     | Reconciler        |
| (replaces current |     | Registry          |
|  FileRule registry|     |                   |
|  + properties     |     | - custom_props    |
|  checker)         |     | - label_sync      |
+-------------------+     | - branch_protect  |
    |                     | - workflow_sync   |
    v                     +-------------------+
+-------------------+           |
| Checker Engine    |<----------+
| (refactored)      |
+-------------------+
    |
    v
+-------------------+
| Webhook Handler   |
| + push event      |
|   handler         |
+-------------------+

docs.title: Rule Types
docs.text:
Rules use the two-label HCL block syntax: rule "<type>" "<name>". The type determines which schema validates the block, and the name is the unique identifier for logging, metrics, and ignore lists.

Rule Type Purpose Check Modes file Ensure a file exists with correct content exists, contains, exact setting Ensure a repo setting has expected value boolean match, string match branch_protection Ensure branch protection rules are set structured comparison

docs.title: File Rule Check Modes
docs.text: Mode Behavior Use Case exists File is present, content ignored Renovate config, catalog-info.yaml contains File is present and passes assertions CODEOWNERS has a real owner, dependabot includes ecosystems exact File must match template (semantic diff for YAML, byte diff for plaintext) CI workflows, standardized configs

docs.title: Content Assertions
docs.text:
Assertions are typed by which field is used:

  • pattern / not_pattern -- regex matching for unstructured files (CODEOWNERS, Makefile, etc.)
  • yaml_path + contains / equals -- YAML-aware path matching, parser inferred from file extension
  • json_path (future) -- JSON-aware path matching

For exact mode, YAML files use semantic comparison (ignore comment/whitespace differences) rather than byte-level diff.

docs.title: Reconciler Types
docs.text:
Reconcilers are optional behaviors attached to rules. They run when a rule's target file exists (or is modified, if watch = true). Each reconciler type has a fixed schema validated at config load time.

Reconciler Type Purpose Fixed Schema Fields custom_properties Read file, extract values, sync to GitHub custom properties mode, owner, component, jira_project, jira_label, defaults label_sync Read labels from file, sync to GitHub repo labels TBD branch_protection Read settings from file, apply branch protection TBD workflow_sync Ensure workflow file matches template TBD

The reconciler interface in Go:

type Reconciler interface {
    // Name returns the reconciler identifier (e.g., "custom_properties").
    Name() string

    // Reconcile is called when the rule's file exists in the repo.
    // content is the file's raw content.
    Reconcile(ctx context.Context, client github.Client,
        owner, repo, defaultBranch, content string) error
}

Adding a new reconciler type requires:

  1. Go code for the reconciler implementation
  2. HCL schema definition for the reconciler's fixed fields
  3. No changes to the rule engine or config loader

docs.title: Ignore Lists
docs.text:
Two levels:

  • Global -- ignore { repos = [...] } at the top level skips repos for all rules
  • Per-rule -- ignore { repos = [...] } inside a rule block skips that specific rule for those repos

Patterns support glob matching (e.g., myorg/terraform-*).

Evaluation order:

  1. Global ignore list checked first (cheapest)
  2. Per-rule ignore list checked before rule evaluation

docs.title: Push Event Handling
docs.text:
When a rule has reconcile { watch = true }, repo-guardian handles push events for the rule's file paths.

The push handler:

  1. Checks the push is to the default branch
  2. Scans commits[].added and commits[].modified for watched file paths
  3. Enqueues the repo if a match is found

This closes the feedback loop where repo-guardian creates a catalog-info.yaml PR, and after merge, immediately reconciles the custom properties rather than waiting for the weekly scheduler.

The GitHub App must subscribe to the push event (one-time manual config). No new permissions are required.

docs.title: Config Loading and Env Var Interaction
docs.text:
The HCL config file is optional. When absent, the system falls back to the current env-var-only behavior, preserving full backward compatibility.

When present, the loading order is:

  1. Built-in defaults (same as today)
  2. guardian.hcl overrides defaults (all settings including operational)
  3. Environment variables override guardian.hcl

This means env vars always win, which is important for Kubernetes deployments where secrets (webhook secret, private key) should never be in the HCL file.

The config file path is set via GUARDIAN_CONFIG env var (default: /etc/repo-guardian/guardian.hcl).

docs.title: Migration from Current System
docs.text:
The refactoring is designed to be non-breaking:

  1. The existing DefaultRules in internal/rules/registry.go become the built-in defaults when no HCL config is present
  2. The existing env vars continue to work unchanged
  3. The custom properties checker logic moves into a custom_properties reconciler but the behavior is identical
  4. The CUSTOM_PROPERTIES_MODE env var continues to work, configuring the built-in catalog_info rule's reconciler

A deployment can migrate incrementally: start using guardian.hcl for new rules and overrides while keeping existing env vars for operational settings.

docs.title: Helm Chart Changes
docs.text:
Add support for mounting guardian.hcl via ConfigMap:

# values.yaml
policy:
  # -- Inline HCL policy configuration
  config: ""
  # -- Use an existing ConfigMap for the policy file
  existingConfigMap: ""

Both inline and external ConfigMap are supported. When policy.config is set, the chart creates a ConfigMap with the HCL content and mounts it at /etc/repo-guardian/guardian.hcl. When policy.existingConfigMap is set, the chart mounts that ConfigMap instead.

docs.title: 1. YAML Configuration File
docs.text: YAML is more universally known, but it lacks HCL's expressiveness for this use case. Policy rules with nested blocks, optional reconcilers, per-rule overrides, and glob patterns are awkward in YAML. YAML also doesn't support comments in a standardized way across all parsers, and doesn't have expressions or references. Since the team already uses HCL for Terraform, the learning curve is zero.

docs.title: 2. CUE
docs.text: CUE provides stronger validation and typing than HCL, but it's less mainstream, has a steeper learning curve, and the Go ecosystem support is less mature. It would be overkill for a configuration file that's essentially a list of rules with optional blocks.

docs.title: 3. Keep Env Vars, Add a JSON/YAML Rules File
docs.text: Split the problem: keep env vars for operational config, add a separate rules file for compliance checks. This avoids the HCL dependency but means two configuration mechanisms that don't compose well. Per-rule overrides and ignore lists would still be awkward in YAML.

docs.title: 4. Go Plugin System (No Config File)
docs.text: Keep rules in Go code but make them more pluggable via interfaces. This maintains type safety but doesn't solve the "add a rule without recompiling" problem. It also doesn't address ignore lists or per-repo overrides.

docs.title: Phase 1: HCL Config Parser and Policy Types
docs.text:
Define the Go types that represent the HCL schema (PolicyConfig, Rule, Reconciler, IgnoreList). Implement the HCL parser using hashicorp/hcl/v2. Write a config loader that supports single file and directory loading, and merges HCL settings with env var overrides.

Deliverable: internal/policy package that can parse guardian.hcl and produce a typed config struct. Comprehensive tests for parsing, validation, env var override behavior, and directory loading.

docs.title: Phase 2: Rule Engine Refactor
docs.text:
Replace the hardcoded FileRule registry with a generic rule engine that reads from the parsed policy config. The checker engine accepts rules from either the policy config or the built-in defaults (when no config file is present). Support all three check modes (exists, contains, exact).

Deliverable: Existing file rules (CODEOWNERS, dependabot, renovate) work identically whether configured via HCL or built-in defaults. Content assertions work for both regex and YAML path matching. All existing tests pass.

docs.title: Phase 3: Reconciler Interface and Custom Properties Migration
docs.text:
Define the Reconciler interface. Migrate the existing custom properties checker into a custom_properties reconciler with a fixed schema. The reconciler is attached to the catalog_info rule and runs when catalog-info.yaml exists.

Deliverable: Custom properties behavior is identical but driven by the reconciler interface. The CUSTOM_PROPERTIES_MODE env var continues to work as a shorthand for configuring the built-in reconciler.

docs.title: Phase 4: Ignore Lists
docs.text:
Implement global and per-rule ignore lists with glob matching. The checker engine checks ignore lists before evaluating rules. Ignore lists are configured in guardian.hcl.

Deliverable: Repos and rules can be excluded via HCL config. Tests cover exact match, glob patterns, global vs per-rule scoping.

docs.title: Phase 5: Push Event Handler
docs.text:
Add push event handling to the webhook handler. When a rule has reconcile { watch = true }, pushes to the default branch that modify the rule's watched files trigger re-evaluation.

Deliverable: Merging a catalog-info.yaml PR triggers an immediate custom properties rescan. Metric: repos_checked_total{trigger="push"}.

docs.title: Phase 6: Additional Rule Types
docs.text:
Implement rule "setting" and rule "branch_protection" types. Define their HCL schemas, checker logic, and reconciler implementations (label_sync, branch_protection, workflow_sync).

Deliverable: Setting and branch protection rules can be declared in guardian.hcl and evaluated by the checker engine.

docs.title: Phase 7: Helm Chart and Documentation
docs.text:
Update the Helm chart to support guardian.hcl via inline values or external ConfigMap. Update documentation, migration guide, and examples.

Deliverable: Users can deploy with HCL config via Helm values. README and chart values document the new configuration model.

docs.title: Risks and Mitigations
docs.text: Risk Impact Likelihood Mitigation HCL dependency adds complexity Medium Low hashicorp/hcl/v2 is a single, stable, well-maintained dependency. It's the same library Terraform uses. Breaking existing deployments High Low HCL config is optional. Existing env-var-only deployments work unchanged. Migration is incremental. Push event volume overwhelms the system Medium Medium Filter in the webhook handler (no API calls). Work queue drops jobs when full. Can remove push event subscription as a kill switch. Over-engineering for current scale Low Medium Phase the implementation. Each phase delivers standalone value. Config file drift between environments Medium Medium Env vars override HCL, so secrets and per-env settings stay in Kubernetes Secrets/ConfigMaps. The HCL file is the same across envs.

docs.title: Resolved Questions
docs.text:
1. Single file vs directory loading: Support both from the start. A single file or a directory of .hcl files. GUARDIAN_CONFIG can point to either.

  2. Operational settings location: All settings (including operational ones like worker_count, schedule_interval) are declared in the HCL file with defaults. Environment variables override any HCL setting.

  3. Reconciler mapping style: Fixed schema per reconciler type. Each reconciler defines its own typed fields (e.g., owner, component, jira_project for custom_properties). Adding new fields requires Go code changes, but validation happens at config load time.

  4. Reconciler types: Four concrete types planned: custom_properties, label_sync, branch_protection, workflow_sync. The interface is justified.

  5. Content validation: Yes, three check modes: exists (presence only), contains (presence + content assertions), exact (must match template). Assertions support regex (pattern / not_pattern) for unstructured files and YAML path matching (yaml_path + contains / equals) for structured files. Parser is inferred from file extension.

  6. Rule types: Design the schema for multiple rule types from the start: rule "file", rule "setting", rule "branch_protection". The two-label HCL block syntax (rule "<type>" "<name>") naturally accommodates this.

  7. Config delivery in Kubernetes: Both inline Helm values (policy.config) and external ConfigMap (policy.existingConfigMap).

docs.title: Success Criteria
docs.text:
• Adding a new file presence rule requires only a guardian.hcl change -- no Go code, no recompile, no redeploy (just a ConfigMap update + rollout)
  • Content assertions catch files that exist but are incorrect (placeholder owners, missing ecosystems)
  • Ignoring a repo or rule for specific repos is a one-line config change
  • catalog-info.yaml changes are detected within seconds of merge (push event handler) rather than up to 168h (scheduler)
  • Existing deployments with env-var-only configuration continue to work unchanged
  • The custom_properties reconciler produces identical behavior to the current special-cased checker
  • Setting and branch protection rules can be declared and enforced via HCL

docs.title: The read-only API
docs.text:
repo-guardian v2 serves a read-only JSON API over the findings store (DESIGN-0027). It backs the business UI and the public status page, and anything else that wants compliance data: a dashboard, a CI gate, a report. Every endpoint is a GET.

The contract is api/openapi.yaml. The running API serves it at /api/v1/openapi.yaml without a token, and every release attaches it as openapi.yaml.

  • Enabling it
  • Authentication
  • Authorization
  • Endpoints
  • The status page
  • Pagination
  • Errors
  • Compatibility

docs.title: Enabling it
docs.text:
api:
  enabled: true
  auth:
    issuer: https://idp.example.com
    audience: repo-guardian-api
  authz:
    groups:
      platform-engineering: ["*"]
      team-web: ["acme"]

In topology split this renders an api Deployment (two replicas and a PDB) and a ClusterIP Service, <release>-repo-guardian-api. In all the API runs inside the one Deployment on api.port and the same Service targets it. The Service is never published by the chart: people reach the API through the UI, and machines from inside the cluster or through an ingress you own.

The API reads Postgres through a read-only role. See the chart README, "The API's read-only role", for how each Postgres mode provides it.

docs.title: Authentication
docs.text:
Every endpoint except /status and /openapi.yaml needs Authorization: Bearer <access token>, an OIDC access token issued for the API's audience. The API:

  • discovers the issuer (api.auth.issuer) and verifies the signature against its JWKS (RS256 or ES256 only);
  • requires iss to equal the issuer exactly and aud to contain api.auth.audience;
  • allows 60 seconds of clock skew on exp and nbf;
  • refuses ID tokens: anything carrying a nonce or at_hash, or a typ claim of ID;
  • reads the caller's name from api.auth.nameClaim (default preferred_username), groups from api.auth.groupsClaim (default groups) and a machine client from api.auth.clientClaim (default azp), each a top-level claim.

Until discovery succeeds the API answers 503 and is not ready. Refusals are counted in repo_guardian_api_auth_failures_total{reason}.

api.auth.enabled: false turns authentication off for a pod-network-only API. The chart then refuses to render the UI or its Ingress (INV-0009).

Setting up a provider, with recipes for the common ones and a checklist for the rest, is in Identity providers.

docs.title: Authorization
docs.text:
api.authz maps groups to the orgs they may see. It is rendered into a ConfigMap, read at startup, and a checksum annotation rolls the API pods when it changes.

api:
  authz:
    groups:
      platform-engineering: ["*"]      # every org
      team-web: ["acme", "acme-labs"]
    defaultOrgs: []                     # for callers matching no group
    clients:
      ci-dashboard: [platform-engineering]
  • A caller sees the union of its groups' orgs. "*" is every org.
  • defaultOrgs applies only when none of the caller's groups is mapped. Leave it empty so an unmapped user sees nothing.
  • clients maps a machine client, by the claim api.auth.clientClaim names, to groups defined above. It is for IdPs that put no groups on client-credentials tokens. Never map the UI's client ID here. Every user token from the UI carries repo-guardian-ui in that claim, so mapping it would grant every signed-in user those groups.
  • Scoping is applied in SQL on every query, including every page of a list. An org the caller cannot see answers 404, the same as one that does not exist. A caller who can see no org gets 403 everywhere except /me, and the UI turns that into an "ask for access" page.

docs.title: Endpoints
docs.text:
All live under /api/v1. The OpenAPI document has the full schemas.

Endpoint Returns /status public service status (below) /me the caller, and the orgs it may see /summary tracked and parked repositories (and parked by reason), the fleet posture, how many controls have a failing result, open PRs, the remediation backlog (reserved, open, recommended or failed), repositories evaluated in the last 24 hours, the active policy version and finding_age: non-compliant results by time since they last changed, in six buckets (<1d, 1-7d, 7-30d, 30-90d, 90-180d, 180d+) that sum to the posture's non_compliant, and open_prs_by_age (<1d, 1-7d, 7-30d, 30d+ by when each was opened) summing to open_prs /controls, /controls/{id} each assigned control's posture (?org= narrows it); one control by org and lineage, with the versions and revisions each org carries /orgs, /orgs/{org} posture and open_prs per org; one org's baseline against what it added (percent and coverage each), its controls, its five worst and its exclusions /repositories, /repositories/{id} repositories filtered by org, active, park_reason, policy_state, q, each with the posture over its own assignments (compliance); one repository with its last evaluation, policy state and whether each App can reach it /repositories/{id}/controls the repository's assignments in remediation order, each with its bucket, mode, rule results, evidence and latest remediation /repositories/{id}/evaluations, /repositories/{id}/events the evaluation log; result changes, repository events and remediation events /results recorded control results across repositories by bucket, control, rule (failing or erroring), org and decision, sorted by last change (since_asc, since_desc) or by open pull request age (pr_age, oldest first, results with none last), each with its failing rules, reason and latest remediation (kind, state, pull request number and URL, age_days); pr_stale=true keeps results whose open pull request is at least 30 days old, false the rest; total on the first page. A finding is a result in the non_compliant bucket, so ?bucket=non_compliant's total is the summary's count /remediations remediations newest first, by kind, state, org, control, hold (repeatable) and older_than_days, each with its proposal and step journal; a branch hold also lists the results held before a pull request exists (below) /remediations/activity pull request throughput: repo-guardian pull requests opened and closed on each UTC day of the last days (1–90, default 14), today included, every day present POST /repositories/{id}/evaluate asks for an evaluation now (below) /compliance/history each UTC day's last snapshot per org, control and lineage, by control, org and days (1–365, default 30); aggregate=fleet, org or control sums each day's rows to one point per day (per org, per control) with the percentages recomputed from the sums /policies the active policy as the caller may see it: its version and rollout, each visible org's layer, the catalogue entries those reference, and the enterprise layer for callers who see every org /openapi.yaml the contract (public)

Posture. Every compliance object is a Posture: one count per bucket (compliant, non-compliant, pending, stale, three unmeasurable reasons, not applicable, unknown, excluded), assigned, and two percentages floored to one decimal. percent is compliant / (compliant + non_compliant); coverage is the measured assignments (compliant, non-compliant, not applicable) over assigned. When the denominator is zero the value is null, never 100, and the UI prints "no data". The API sums rows and recomputes both from the sums, exactly as the SQL does, so no total is an average of percentages.

Evidence explains a rule result. Each object carries evidence_kind (<control type>.<rule kind>) and evidence_version; framework evidence, written when an evaluation could not decide, adds reason. Values in it came from repositories (paths, file contents, setting values): treat them as data and never render them as markup.

Remediations. /remediations lists one row per remediation: a pull request (reserved through merged or a close), a recommendation, or a direct apply with its proposal (each resource's value before and the value asked for) and steps journal. Open pull requests older than N days are ?kind=pull_request&state=open&older_than_days=N, outstanding recommendations ?state=recommended, blocked cleanup ?hold=permission. The branch holds (pr_cap, foreign_branch, stale_branch, conflict) are set on a result before any pull request exists, so ?hold= with one of them also lists those results as rows of their own: kind pull_request, no id, state or pull request, and created_at when the hold began. One cursor pages both kinds of row.

Re-evaluation. POST /repositories/{id}/evaluate signals the repository's evaluation workflow at the highest priority and answers 202. It is the API's only write and touches no table. Visibility comes first (404, as for the GET). An API replica with no Temporal client answers 501, and the UI hides its button; set api.temporal in the chart to give the api role one. A parked repository is 409 with type parked, and one with no running workflow 409 workflow_missing. Each replica sends at most one signal per repository per minute and answers 202 to the rest.

curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  "https://guardian.example.com/api/v1/controls?org=acme"

docs.title: The status page
docs.text: GET /api/v1/status is public when api.status.public is true (the default). It reports an overall state, one state per component (checks, webhooks, discovery, snapshots, and backlog_evaluation / backlog_remediation for each queue whose App is configured) with a fixed-template detail such as "last success 3m ago", the deployment's topology (split or all), and apps: each App with an installation and its installation, suspended and reachable-repository counts. compliance carries the fleet percent and coverage and compliance.history: one point per UTC day over the last 30 days, taken from that day's last snapshot. operations adds repositories evaluated in the last 24 hours, remediation_backlog (outstanding remediations, as on /summary), overdue (managed repositories with no successful evaluation within twice EVAL_INTERVAL), tracked repositories, the newest policy version's rollout_state (none, in_progress or complete, with rollout_completed_at) and last_snapshot_at. It names no org, repository, control or installation and carries no error text. The API computes it every 30 seconds in memory, so a request never reaches the database.

docs.title: Pagination
docs.text:
Lists return items and, when there is more, next_cursor. Pass it back unchanged as ?cursor=, with the same filters, to get the next page. limit defaults to 50 and is capped at 200.

Cursors are keyset positions, not offsets, so pages stay stable while checks write. A cursor is bound to the filters it was issued with: sending it with different filters is a 400. Cursors are opaque and unsigned. Tampering with one cannot widen what you see, because scoping is applied to every page.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text:
Errors are RFC 9457 application/problem+json:

{"type": "about:blank", "title": "Not Found", "status": 404, "detail": "no such org", "request_id": "c0ffee…"}
Status When 400 a malformed filter, limit or cursor, or a cursor from other filters 401 no token, or a token that fails verification; carries WWW-Authenticate: Bearer 403 the caller can see no org 404 no such resource, or one in an org the caller cannot see 503 the issuer has not been discovered yet

request_id matches the API's logs. Quote it when reporting a problem.

docs.title: Compatibility
docs.text:
/api/v1 changes only additively:

  • new endpoints, new optional query parameters and new response fields may appear;
  • enums documented as open (status, reason, remediation, park reason, trigger, component) may gain values, so treat an unknown value as opaque rather than failing;
  • nothing is removed or renamed, and no field changes type.

The contract's info.version follows semver: an addition bumps the minor version. 2.0.0 is the controls line (IMPL-0029): the findings endpoints (/rules, /findings, /policy, /installations, /repositories/{id}/checks) are gone, replaced by /controls, /policies, /repositories/{id}/controls and /repositories/{id}/evaluations, and every compliance object is a Posture. It ships before v2.0.0 is released, so no 1.x client exists to break.

2.1.0 (IMPL-0030) adds remediation: /remediations, /remediations/activity and /results; aggregate on /compliance/history; compliance on every repository; each assignment's latest remediation on /repositories/{id}/controls; remediation events in the timeline; and on /summary remediation_backlog, parked_by_reason, controls_failing, finding_age and open_prs_by_age (the status page gains remediation_backlog). On a rule-level event (rule_id set), from_status and to_status are rule statuses (pass, fail, error, unknown, not applicable), not result statuses.

Anything else would be /api/v2, served beside v1 for a deprecation window. The UI and the API are released together from one tag, so the UI always matches its API.
