docs.title: Getting started with repo-guardian
docs.text:
A fresh install of repo-guardian 2.0.0, from nothing to a first evaluation, then remediation on one organisation. Each step is short and links to the page that has the full detail. For what repo-guardian enforces and why, read repo-guardian and v2 at a glance. For the complete install runbook, read Turning on repo-guardian v2.

[!NOTE] A new install writes nothing to GitHub. It reads every repository, records each control's result and reports compliance. Pull requests start only when an assignment is in mode = "remediate" on a repository the Remediation App can reach.

  • 1. What you need
  • 2. Create the two GitHub Apps
  • 3. Write a minimal policy
  • 4. Write the values file and install
  • 5. The first evaluation
  • 6. Reading the UI
  • 7. Turning on remediation for one organisation
  • 8. Next steps

docs.title: 1. What you need
docs.text:
• A Kubernetes cluster and a namespace for repo-guardian (repo-guardian below).
  • Helm, able to pull OCI charts from ghcr.io.
  • A Temporal cluster you run. Every evaluation is a Temporal workflow, so Temporal is required. repo-guardian does not ship it. You need server 1.31 or newer, a namespace (default repo-guardian), network access to the frontend on port 7233, and mTLS or OIDC credentials. See A Temporal cluster.
  • Postgres. Pick one with store.postgres.mode:
  • baked (the default): the chart runs a single Postgres pod. Good for a trial.
  • cnpg: the chart renders a CloudNativePG cluster. Needs the CNPG operator.
  • external: you provide an empty database and a DSN Secret, for example on RDS.

See Postgres. - A public HTTPS route to the ingest Service, so GitHub can deliver webhooks. The chart ships no webhook Ingress; pick an option from webhook ingress.

docs.title: 2. Create the two GitHub Apps
docs.text:
repo-guardian runs as two GitHub Apps. The private key is the security boundary: the process that only reads holds a key that cannot write.

Evaluation App Remediation App Access read-only writes Key held by the evaluator the remediator Install on every organisation the policy manages only organisations you remediate Webhook URL https://<your host>/webhooks/github/eval https://<your host>/webhooks/github/remediate Needed for everything remediation only

Create the Evaluation App now. The Remediation App can wait until step 7.

For each App:

  1. Register it with its webhook active, pointing at its URL above. Generate a strong webhook secret.
  2. Grant its permissions and subscribe to its events:
  3. Evaluation App: a fixed read-only set (Metadata, Contents, Pull requests, Administration, and organisation Custom properties, all read), subscribed to Push, Repository, Installation repositories and Pull request. The evaluator logs the set at startup as Evaluation App permissions required. The full table is in Evaluation App permissions.
  4. Remediation App: derived from your policy. The base set is Metadata read, Contents write and Pull requests write. A control that writes through the API with apply = "direct" adds write on its resource, and a control that writes under .github/workflows/ adds Workflows write. The remediator logs the set it needs at startup as Remediation App permissions required, with the list in the permissions field. Subscribe it to Installation repositories only. See Remediation App permissions.
  5. Generate a private key.
  6. Install it. The Evaluation App goes into every organisation the policy lists.

Put each App's key and webhook secret in a Secret with the keys private-key and webhook-secret:

kubectl -n repo-guardian create secret generic rg-eval-app \
  --from-file=private-key=./eval.pem \
  --from-literal=webhook-secret="$EVAL_WEBHOOK_SECRET"

Installing across many organisations is covered in the enterprise setup guide. Use the permission tables in the onboarding runbook in place of its single-App table.

docs.title: 3. Write a minimal policy
docs.text:
The policy is a directory:

policy/
├── enterprise.hcl     # the organisations, the baseline controls, the default mode
├── catalogue/*.hcl    # one control definition per file
├── orgs/*.hcl         # optional per-organisation layers
└── templates/         # optional template overrides

Start small and in evaluate. This is examples/policy/minimal with the mode set to evaluate:

# enterprise.hcl
enterprise {
  orgs     = ["myorg"]
  mode     = "evaluate"
  controls = ["codeowners@1", "dependabot@1"]
}

# catalogue/codeowners.hcl
control "codeowners" {
  version     = 1
  type        = "codeowners"
  title       = "CODEOWNERS"
  description = "A CODEOWNERS file exists in one of GitHub's locations"
  template    = "codeowners"

  rule "exists" {
    title     = "A CODEOWNERS file exists"
    remediate = true
  }
}

# catalogue/dependabot.hcl
control "dependabot" {
  version     = 1
  type        = "dependency_updates"
  title       = "Dependabot"
  description = "Dependabot version updates are configured"
  template    = "dependabot"
  tool        = "dependabot"

  rule "configured" {
    title     = "A Dependabot config exists"
    remediate = true
  }
}
  • enterprise.orgs is the onboarding list. A repository in any other organisation is discovered but unmanaged, so nothing is evaluated on it.
  • enterprise.controls is the baseline: every listed organisation gets these controls, as slug@version.
  • mode is evaluate (record results, change nothing) or remediate. Unset means evaluate.
  • remediate = true on a rule means remediation may fix it. It does nothing while the mode is evaluate.
  • The codeowners and dependabot templates are built in. Put a file under templates/ only to override one.

To leave some repositories out, add an org layer. Every exclusion carries a reason, which the report, the API and the UI show:

# orgs/myorg.hcl
org "myorg" {
  exclude_repos {
    match  = [".github", "archive-*"]
    reason = "org config and archives are managed elsewhere"
  }
}

Check the policy before you deploy it. monitoring generate runs the same loader and validation as the server and fails on any error:

repo-guardian monitoring generate --config ./policy --out /tmp/check

The policy reference has every attribute and block, and the control-type reference has every built-in control type.

docs.title: 4. Write the values file and install
docs.text:
A minimal values file for a split install with the baked Postgres:

# values.yaml
topology: split                      # one Deployment per role (the default)

temporal:
  address: temporal-frontend.temporal.svc:7233
  namespace: repo-guardian
  tls:
    existingSecret: repo-guardian-temporal-tls   # tls.crt, tls.key, ca.crt

github:
  eval:
    appId: "123456"
    existingSecret: rg-eval-app      # private-key, webhook-secret

store:
  postgres:
    mode: baked

evalInterval: "24h"                  # how often each repository is re-evaluated

policy:
  files:
    enterprise.hcl: |
      enterprise {
        orgs     = ["myorg"]
        mode     = "evaluate"
        controls = ["codeowners@1", "dependabot@1"]
      }
    catalogue:
      codeowners.hcl: |
        control "codeowners" {
          version     = 1
          type        = "codeowners"
          title       = "CODEOWNERS"
          description = "A CODEOWNERS file exists in one of GitHub's locations"
          template    = "codeowners"

          rule "exists" {
            title     = "A CODEOWNERS file exists"
            remediate = true
          }
        }
      dependabot.hcl: |
        control "dependabot" {
          version     = 1
          type        = "dependency_updates"
          title       = "Dependabot"
          description = "Dependabot version updates are configured"
          template    = "dependabot"
          tool        = "dependabot"

          rule "configured" {
            title     = "A Dependabot config exists"
            remediate = true
          }
        }

Notes on the values:

  • temporal: with OIDC instead of mTLS, set temporal.auth.oidc.tokenUrl, clientId and existingSecret in place of temporal.tls.existingSecret.
  • github.eval: the evaluator renders only when appId is set. Without existingSecret the chart creates the Secret from privateKey and webhookSecret, which is fine for a trial.
  • store.postgres.mode: with baked under GitOps, set store.postgres.baked.existingSecret, or the generated password changes on every helm template. With external, set store.postgres.existingSecret to a Secret holding STORE_DSN. For separate evaluator and remediator database roles, see Controls database roles.
  • policy.files: the policy directory as a nested map. A string is a file, a map is a directory. The chart mounts it at /etc/repo-guardian/policy and points GUARDIAN_CONFIG at it. To manage the ConfigMap yourself, set policy.existingConfigMap instead. examples/values-with-policy.yaml is a larger example.

Install:

helm upgrade --install repo-guardian \
  oci://ghcr.io/donaldgifford/charts/repo-guardian \
  --version 2.0.0 -n repo-guardian -f values.yaml

The migrate Job runs first. It creates the schema and activates the policy's version. Then the ingest and evaluator pods start. With Argo CD, read Installing with Argo CD first.

docs.title: 5. The first evaluation
docs.text:
Once the evaluator is up:

  1. It creates the controls-discovery schedule and runs it. Discovery lists every installation of the Evaluation App and every repository in it.
  2. Each managed repository gets one evaluation/<repository id> workflow. It evaluates the repository's controls, records the results, and sleeps until the next evaluation.
  3. First evaluations are spread across evalInterval (24h by default), so a large fleet does not drain the GitHub rate limit at once. A repository that is created, or pushed to on a path a control reads, is evaluated straight away.

Check it:

  • Pods. kubectl -n repo-guardian get pods shows ingest and the evaluator Ready, and the migrate Job completed.
  • Permissions. The evaluator's startup log has Evaluation App permissions required. Compare it with what the installation granted.
  • Webhooks. Push to a repository, then open the Evaluation App's Advanced → Recent Deliveries. 202 means started, 204 means nothing to do, 401 means the webhook secret does not match, and 503 means Temporal is unreachable.
  • Temporal. In the Temporal UI, a controls-discovery run has completed and there is one evaluation/<id> workflow per managed repository.
  • One repository, from your machine. repo-guardian evaluate runs the policy against one repository as the Evaluation App, with no database and no Temporal:

bash EVAL_GITHUB_APP_ID=123456 EVAL_GITHUB_PRIVATE_KEY_PATH=./eval.pem \ repo-guardian evaluate --repo myorg/service-a --policy ./policy

--policy defaults to $GUARDIAN_CONFIG, and --format json prints the full result. It exits 0 when compliant (or when nothing was measured), 1 when non-compliant, 2 on a usage error and 3 on an operational one. - Status. /status on the API (/api/v1/status), or the UI's status page, shows overall health with no login and no names.

docs.title: 6. Reading the UI
docs.text:
The UI is optional. It needs the API (api.enabled), an OIDC identity provider and a few Secrets; the business UI covers enabling it and identity providers covers the provider setup.

Once it is up:

  • Fleet (/) is the overview: compliance, the worst controls, and parked repositories.
  • Findings lists every non-compliant result, oldest first.
  • Controls, Orgs and Repositories drill into one control, one organisation or one repository, with each rule's result and evidence.
  • Policy shows the active policy version and its rollout.

Compliance reads "no data" when nothing is measured, never 100%. Remediation panels read "Remediation is not enabled on this deployment" until you add the Remediation App.

docs.title: 7. Turning on remediation for one organisation
docs.text:
Do this for one organisation, watch it, then widen it.

  1. Create and install the Remediation App on that organisation only, with its webhook at /webhooks/github/remediate (step 2). Store its key and webhook secret in a Secret, rg-remediate-app below.
  2. Add it to the values and upgrade:

yaml github: remediate: appId: "234567" existingSecret: rg-remediate-app # private-key, webhook-secret

The chart now renders the remediator Deployment and mounts the Remediation App's key into it alone. Compare its Remediation App permissions required log line with what the installation granted. 3. Wait for access. The remediator's controls-discovery-remediate schedule records which repositories the App can reach. Until then, that organisation's assignments stay in evaluate, with the reason remediation_app_no_access. 4. Set the mode in that organisation's layer, and deploy the policy:

hcl # orgs/myorg.hcl org "myorg" { mode = "remediate" }

The most specific mode wins, so you can go narrower: a repos block or a single control "<slug@N>" { mode = "remediate" } override. See Resolution.

What the pull requests look like:

  • One pull request per control, on the branch repo-guardian/<control slug>, updated in place as results change.
  • A cap per repository. remediation { max_open_prs } (default 3) limits how many are open at once. The rest wait, held as pr_cap.
  • Humans win. You can push to a repo-guardian pull request. The remediator merges the default branch into it and keeps your edits. It never force-pushes; a branch it cannot update cleanly is held as conflict.
  • It closes what it opened, when the control passes on the default branch or is no longer assigned, with a comment.
  • It never deletes a branch. Not after a merge, not after a close. Use the repository's delete_branch_on_merge setting for cleanup.

When nothing happens, the UI's Remediations page says why, as a hold. How it fixes things explains each hold and how it clears.

To pause, set mode = "evaluate" again and deploy the policy. Evaluation continues, and no new pull requests open.

docs.title: 8. Next steps
docs.text:
• Policy reference: every attribute and block in the policy directory, and how a repository's assignments resolve.
  • Control-type reference: every built-in control type and its parameters.
  • repo-guardian and v2 at a glance: the model behind controls, modes and remediation.
  • Identity providers: OIDC setup for the API and the UI.
  • Scaling: sizing, rate limits and the compliance metrics.

docs.title: Policy reference (policy directory)
docs.text:
The specification of repo-guardian's controls policy: the files in the policy directory, the blocks and attributes each one holds, how a repository's controls are resolved, and what fails load. The attributes of each control type live in the generated Control-type reference; this page does not repeat them.

Source of truth: internal/policy/ (load.go, enterprise.go, org.go, catalogue.go, layers.go, resolve.go, validate.go, ownership.go). When this page and the loader disagree, the loader wins.

The worked examples are the policy roots under examples/policy/. Every one of them is loaded by the test suite, so the snippets quoted below parse as written.

Example What it shows examples/policy/minimal one org, two baseline controls examples/policy/full every built-in control type once, exclude_repos and a repos block examples/policy/multi-org two orgs adding different controls, one of them evaluate-only examples/policy/enterprise several orgs using replace, exclude, modes and remediation settings examples/policy/renovate Renovate in place of Dependabot

docs.title: The policy directory
docs.text:
GUARDIAN_CONFIG names the policy root, a directory. Ingest, both controls workers and the migrate Job read it. The layout is fixed:

<root>/
  enterprise.hcl        # required: exactly one enterprise block
  catalogue/*.hcl       # control definitions
  orgs/*.hcl            # one org block per managed org that varies the baseline
  templates/            # optional: file and PR templates the catalogue names
  • enterprise.hcl must exist at the root.
  • catalogue/ and orgs/ hold .hcl files one level deep. File names are free; the blocks inside decide what they mean.
  • Any other .hcl file anywhere under the root fails load.
  • Files that are not .hcl are not parsed. They can still be read with file() or as templates.
  • Size limit: every file is capped at 1 MiB, and the whole root has to fit one ConfigMap.

The root is read once at startup. There is no hot reload: a change takes effect when the process restarts.

docs.title: Expressions: literals and file()
docs.text:
Attribute values are literals: strings, numbers, booleans, lists and objects. The one function is file("<path>"), which returns the content of a file under the root.

  • The path is relative to the root and must stay inside it. An absolute path or a .. that leaves the root fails load.
  • file() reads from the same pass as everything else, so the file is part of the policy version.

There are no variables, no locals and no other functions.

docs.title: Symlinks and the kubelet ..data layout
docs.text:
The root may be a ConfigMap projection.

  • Symlinks: every file is resolved with EvalSymlinks and must land inside the resolved root. A link that escapes the root fails load.
  • ..data: when the root holds kubelet's ..data link, the loader walks that one consistent snapshot.
  • Names starting with ..: skipped either way.

With the Helm chart, policy.files is the root as a nested map: a string is a file, a map is a directory. Each file is mounted back at its path. policy.existingConfigMap mounts an existing ConfigMap instead.

policy:
  files:
    enterprise.hcl: |
      enterprise { ... }
    catalogue:
      codeowners.hcl: |
        control "codeowners" { ... }
    orgs:
      myorg.hcl: |
        org "myorg" { ... }

docs.title: Templates
docs.text:
A control's template = "<name>" resolves in this order:

  1. templates/<name>.tmpl under the policy root.
  2. templates/<name> under the policy root.
  3. The embedded template of that name.

The root's templates override the embedded ones per policy. The embedded templates a policy uses are hashed into its version, so upgrading the binary with a changed embedded template counts as a policy change. examples/policy/enterprise/templates/codeowners-team.tmpl is a root template that codeowners@2 names.

docs.title: The policy version
docs.text:
The loaded policy has a version: controls: followed by a sha256 over these inputs:

  • every file under the root;
  • the embedded templates used;
  • every definition's revision.

The migrate Job activates the version, and a new version starts a rollout that re-evaluates the fleet. Editing a comment is a new version.

docs.title: enterprise.hcl
docs.text:
enterprise {
  orgs     = ["myorg-prod", "myorg-staging"]
  mode     = "remediate"
  controls = ["codeowners@1", "dependabot@1"]
}
Attribute / block Type Required Meaning orgs list(string) yes The orgs repo-guardian manages. This list is onboarding: an org not listed is unmanaged, whatever else the policy says. mode string no evaluate or remediate. The fallback mode for every assignment. Unset means evaluate. controls list(string) no The baseline: slug@version references into the catalogue. Every listed org gets them, with or without a file under orgs/. remediation {} block no max_open_prs (number, at least 1) and reopen_after (duration string, at least 1h).

The enterprise policy is the baseline and has no variations: exclude, replace, exclude_repos, repos and control blocks are refused here with an error that says so.

Remediation settings resolve org, then enterprise, then the default: max_open_prs = 3, reopen_after = "336h".

docs.title: catalogue/*.hcl
docs.text:
A catalogue file holds control blocks. Each one defines one version of one control.

control "codeowners" {
  version     = 1
  type        = "codeowners"
  title       = "CODEOWNERS"
  description = "A CODEOWNERS file exists in one of GitHub's locations"
  template    = "codeowners"

  rule "exists" {
    number    = "1.1"
    title     = "A CODEOWNERS file exists"
    remediate = true
  }

  pr {
    title = "chore({{ .Repo }}): adopt CODEOWNERS"
  }
}

The slug is the block label. It matches ^[a-z][a-z0-9]*([_-][a-z0-9]+)*$. A control is referenced everywhere else as slug@version, for example codeowners@1. One slug may have several versions in the catalogue (examples/policy/enterprise/catalogue/codeowners.hcl defines @1 and @2). The same slug@version defined twice fails load.

Attribute / block Required Meaning version yes A positive integer. type yes A built-in control type (see the Control-type reference). An unknown type fails load. title, description no Display text. template no The template the type renders for remediation (see Templates). rule "<id>" {} per type One typed check. remediation { apply = "…" } no How an API type writes: recommend, direct or, where the type supports it, workflow. pr {} no Pull request text: title, body (templates, compiled at load) and labels. any other attribute per type A control-level parameter of the type, e.g. path on file, tool and renovate on dependency_updates, name and ruleset on branch_ruleset, annotation_properties and properties on custom_properties. The type validates them when it builds the definition.

docs.title: Rules
docs.text:
rule "no-wiki" {
  kind      = "equals"
  property  = "has_wiki"
  value     = false
  remediate = true
}
  • The id is the block label. It follows the slug pattern and is unique within the control.
  • kind is one of the type's rule kinds. A rule without kind takes its id as its kind, which works only when the id is a kind of that type (rule "exists", rule "matches").
  • remediate = true asks for the rule to be fixed in remediate mode. It is allowed only on a remediable kind.
  • number and title are display text.
  • Any other attribute is a parameter of the rule kind. Unknown parameters, missing required ones and wrong types fail load. The per-kind parameter tables are in the Control-type reference.

docs.title: apply is for API types only
docs.text:
Pull request types (file, codeowners, catalog_info, dependency_updates) remediate by pull request and refuse an apply value. API types (repo_settings, branch_ruleset, labels, custom_properties) take one.

  • recommend reports the change without making it.
  • direct writes it through the Remediation App.
  • workflow is accepted only by a type that supports it (today custom_properties).

docs.title: A definition must pass its own template
docs.text:
At load, each definition goes through a dry run:

  1. Evaluate an empty repository.
  2. Remediate it.
  3. Apply the rendered files.
  4. Evaluate again.

A remediable rule that the rendered template leaves non-compliant fails load. A template that cannot fix what it is meant to fix never reaches a repository.

docs.title: orgs/*.hcl
docs.text:
An org file holds org "<name>" blocks. A missing org file is fine: every org in enterprise.orgs gets the baseline as it is.

  • Org names compare case-insensitively, as GitHub logins do.
  • An org not in enterprise.orgs fails load. Onboarding is the enterprise list.
  • Each org has at most one block, across all files.
org "myorg" {
  exclude_repos {
    match  = [".github", "terraform-*", "archive-*"]
    reason = "org config, infrastructure and archives are managed elsewhere"
  }

  repos "legacy" {
    match = ["legacy-*"]

    exclude "protect_main@1" {
      reason = "legacy repositories predate the review policy"
    }
  }
}
Attribute / block In org In repos Meaning mode yes yes evaluate or remediate for this layer. controls yes yes Controls this layer adds, as slug@version. replace "<slug@N>" { with, reason } yes yes Swap an assigned control for another. with is required. exclude "<slug@N>" { reason } yes yes Turn an assigned control off. control "<slug@N>" { mode } yes yes Set the mode of one control. mode is required. exclude_repos { match, reason } yes no Take matching repositories out of management entirely. match is required. repos "<label>" { match, … } yes no A group of repositories with its own layer. match is required. remediation {} yes no Overrides the enterprise's max_open_prs / reopen_after.

replace, exclude and exclude_repos must carry a non-empty reason. The reason is recorded on the assignment and shown in the report, the API and the UI.

match is a list of globs (Go path.Match syntax) against the repository name without its org, compared case-insensitively. examples/policy/enterprise/orgs/ shows replace (payments.hcl), exclude with exclude_repos (sandbox.hcl) and a repos block narrowing the mode (platform.hcl).

docs.title: Resolution
docs.text:
Each repository is resolved from its stored row and the two Apps' access to it. Resolution makes no API calls. Snapshot.Resolve implements steps 1–6 below; step 7, the assignment epochs, belongs to the store. The results are pinned by the goldens in internal/policy/testdata/resolution.

Before the steps:

  • Unmanaged: a repository whose org is not in enterprise.orgs has no assignments.
  • Excluded: a repository matching an exclude_repos block of its org is excluded, with that block's reason, and has no assignments. The first matching block wins.
  • Parked: an inactive repository (archived, fork, removed, access lost) still resolves, so its assignments are known, but its state is parked.

Everything else is managed. The steps:

  1. Baseline. Every control in enterprise.controls is assigned with decision baseline, in list order.
  2. Layers. The org layer applies, then each repos block whose match covers the repository, in file order. Within one layer the operations apply in the order they appear in the file:
  3. controls adds a control. An exclude of the same control in the same layer beats the addition.
  4. replace swaps an active control for with. The replacement keeps the source's place and lineage, with decision replaced.
  5. exclude marks an active control excluded, with decision excluded and its reason. The assignment row stays, so the exclusion is visible.
  6. One row per slug. Each slug has at most one assignment.
  7. Adding another version of a slug that is already assigned replaces that row in place.
  8. A slug the enterprise names stays baseline, whichever version is assigned.
  9. A slug only an org or block adds is org_added.
  10. Requested mode. The first of these that is set wins:
  11. a control {} override in a matching repos block;
  12. that block's mode;
  13. an org-level control {} override;
  14. the org mode;
  15. the enterprise mode;
  16. evaluate.

Among matching repos blocks the later one in the file wins. The assignment records which layer decided (mode_source). 5. Effective mode. Usually the requested mode. A remediate request drops to evaluate when the Remediation App cannot reach the repository: - no access gives mode_reason = "remediation_app_no_access"; - a suspended installation gives remediation_app_suspended.

Evaluation never depends on the Remediation App. 6. Conflicts. Two active assignments that own the same resource, for example two controls writing one file or one ruleset, both become conflict. Each carries an error naming the resource and the claimants. A conflicting assignment is not evaluated; compliance reports it as unmeasurable.

In examples/policy/multi-org:

  • Repositories in myorg-prod get codeowners@1 and dependabot@1 as baseline, plus protect_main_strict@1 and catalog_info@1 as org_added. All four are in remediate, from the enterprise.
  • In myorg-staging the org's mode = "evaluate" covers both its baseline and protect_main@1.

docs.title: Validation
docs.text:
Load collects every error, joins them and fails. Each error carries file:line. Warnings are logged once at load and do not stop it.

Fails load:

  • A layout problem:
  • no enterprise.hcl;
  • an .hcl file outside the three places;
  • a file over 1 MiB, not a regular file, or resolving outside the root;
  • a file() path outside the root or missing.
  • HCL that does not parse, an unknown block or attribute where the schema is closed, or an expression other than a literal or file().
  • More than one enterprise block, or a variation block inside it.
  • An org block for an org not in enterprise.orgs, or a second block for the same org.
  • A catalogue problem:
  • an invalid slug or rule id;
  • version below 1;
  • an unknown type;
  • a slug@version defined twice;
  • an unknown rule kind;
  • a rule without kind whose id is not a kind;
  • remediate = true on a kind that is not remediable;
  • an unknown, missing or mistyped parameter;
  • a bad apply;
  • a PR template that does not parse;
  • a template that fails its own remediable rules.
  • A reference to a control or version the catalogue lacks. The error lists the versions that exist.
  • A mode other than evaluate or remediate.
  • max_open_prs below 1, or a reopen_after that is not a duration of at least 1h.
  • replace, exclude or exclude_repos without a reason.
  • Two repos blocks with one label in an org, or a glob that does not parse.
  • A replace whose source is not assigned at that layer. For a repos block, "at that layer" means the org result plus whatever earlier blocks add.
  • A replace whose two controls own no resource in common.
  • A control {} override naming a control no layer of the org assigns.

Warns only:

  • An exclude of a control not assigned at that layer, since it does nothing.
  • One control's mode declared twice in one scope with different values. The later declaration wins.
  • Two repos blocks whose globs may overlap and that declare different modes, block-wide or for one control. The later block wins.
  • A repos block that re-adds a control an earlier overlapping block excluded. Block order decides.
  • Ownership overlaps. For every org the loader resolves:
  • the org layer alone;
  • the org layer with each repos block;
  • the org layer with each pair of repos blocks.

It warns when two active controls would own the same resource. These are warnings because which blocks a repository meets is unknown until discovery. Resolution step 6 is the authority, and a real overlap shows up there as a conflict assignment. - After discovery: a repos block that matches no known repository.

To load a policy without starting a worker, run repo-guardian monitoring generate --config <root> --out <dir>. It runs the same policy.Load and fails with the same errors.

docs.title: From guardian.hcl
docs.text:
There is no automatic translation (DESIGN-0029 D1). v1 rules described paths and regexes; controls are typed checks, and a mechanical translation would produce generic file controls and lose what the types know. Rewrite a v1 policy by hand with this table. The examples/policy/ roots are the v1 examples rewritten: minimal, full, multi-org and renovate each name the v1 file they replace in their enterprise.hcl comment.

v1 Controls rule "file" with check = "exists" a file control, rule "exists": one path, one template. Prefer a dedicated type where one exists (codeowners knows every location GitHub reads it from). rule "file" with check = "exact" a file control, rule "exact" (examples/policy/full/catalogue/renovate_workflow.hcl). rule "file" with check = "contains" and assertion {} blocks the dedicated type that owns the file, whose rules are the typed checks: codeowners, catalog_info (field_set, annotation_set, no_placeholders), dependency_updates (configured, extends). check = "absent" and when { rule_satisfied } absorbed by the type that owns the opinion. "No Dependabot config once Renovate is configured" is dependency_updates' exclusive rule (examples/policy/renovate). rule "setting" repo_settings, one equals rule per property, remediated through the API. rule "branch_protection" and the branch_protection reconciler one branch_ruleset control (exists, matches) with the ruleset declared inline. reconcile "custom_properties" a custom_properties control reading catalog-info.yaml; annotation_properties keeps its v1 meaning. mode = "github-action" becomes remediation { apply = "workflow" }. reconcile "label_sync" a labels control, one present or absent rule per label. reconcile "workflow_sync" nothing. Its only job was feeding the push-watched path set; every control now declares what it owns and reads, and a push re-evaluates only the controls it touched. top-level scope {} and rule scope {} enterprise.orgs for the org universe, and org files that add, replace or exclude controls per org (examples/policy/multi-org). global and rule ignore {} exclude_repos for whole repositories, or exclude in a repos block for one control (examples/policy/full/orgs/myorg.hcl). Every exclusion now needs a reason. pr {} at defaults / rule / reconcile scope a pr {} block on the control definition. PRs are per control, on branch repo-guardian/<slug>, so there is no multi-rule bundle. dry_run / DRY_RUN mode = "evaluate", at enterprise, org, repos block or single-control scope. guardian { skip_forks, skip_archived } not policy. Archived repositories and forks are parked by the runtime. templates.files in the chart templates/ under the policy root.

docs.title: The business UI
docs.text:
The UI (DESIGN-0027) shows compliance to people who are not operators: where the fleet stands, which rules fail and where, and what repo-guardian is doing about it. It is read-only and shows the API's data scoped to your groups. Operators keep Grafana for the service itself.

  • Enabling it
  • The shell
  • Views
  • Sessions
  • Rotating session keys
  • Security properties

docs.title: Enabling it
docs.text:
The UI needs the API with authentication on (see the API):

api:
  enabled: true
  auth:
    issuer: https://idp.example.com
  authz:
    groups:
      team-web: ["acme"]
ui:
  enabled: true
  existingSecret: repo-guardian-ui
  docsUrl: https://docs.example.com/repo-guardian   # optional: the sidebar Docs link
  ingress:
    enabled: true
    className: nginx
    host: guardian.example.com
    tls:
      - hosts: [guardian.example.com]
        secretName: guardian-tls

The Secret holds the OIDC client secret and the session keys:

kubectl -n repo-guardian create secret generic repo-guardian-ui \
  --from-literal=oidc-client-secret="$CLIENT_SECRET" \
  --from-literal=session-keys="$(openssl rand -base64 48)"

The UI signs users in against api.auth.issuer with the confidential client ui.oidc.clientId (default repo-guardian-ui). Setting up the client on your provider is in Identity providers. The redirect URI is <public URL>/auth/callback, where the public URL is ui.publicUrl or https://<ui.ingress.host>.

The Ingress is the only one the chart renders, and it sends the whole host to the UI. The webhook route stays yours; see webhook ingress.

docs.title: The shell
docs.text:
Every signed-in page shares one frame (DESIGN-0036):

  • Sidebar. Business holds Fleet, Findings (with the count of non-compliant results in scope), Controls, Orgs, Repositories, Remediations (with the outstanding count; blank without the Remediation App), History and Policy. Public holds the status page. A Docs group with one Documentation link appears only when ui.docsUrl is set. Below 900px the sidebar collapses behind a menu button in the top bar.
  • Time zone. The Local / UTC toggle in the top bar sets how every timestamp prints. The choice is kept in the browser (localStorage key rg.tz), never sent to the server.
  • Account menu. The avatar names you and holds Sign out.
  • Breadcrumbs above every page title, ending at the control, org or repository you are on. A repository reads org/name (… for the moment it is loading), never its numeric id.

docs.title: Views
docs.text:
View Path Shows Fleet / the compliance card (tracked, compliant % with its move over the range, non-compliant, parked, snapshots; series pills ?series= choosing compliance %, findings, not applicable or unknown from aggregate=fleet history), finding age, the five worst controls with their deltas, parked by reason, assignments by bucket, compliance by control with a sparkline per row from one aggregate=control request, the orgs (or one org's exclusions under ?org=), and — with the Remediation App — open PRs by age and PR throughput over 14 days Findings /findings every non-compliant result: the repository, the control, its failing rules and reason, its remediation and how long it has failed. Filters map 1:1 to GET /results (?control=, ?rule=, ?org=, ?decision=, ?pr_stale=), sorted oldest first (?sort=since_desc, ?sort=pr_age with the Remediation App); ?open=<repository id>/<control> opens the finding's drawer — its rules, evidence, timeline, last evaluations and Re-evaluate Remediations /remediations what repo-guardian is doing about findings (needs the Remediation App; otherwise the page reads "Remediation is not enabled on this deployment" and the nav count is blank): KPIs for open PRs (with the stale count), recommendations, held results by reason and failed applies; the views All / Open PRs / Recommendations / Held / Failed (?view=); chips mapping 1:1 to GET /remediations (?kind=, ?state=, ?org=, ?control=, ?hold=, ?older_than= days); ?open=<remediation id> (or <repository id>/<control> for a held result) opens the drawer — state, the pull request and its repo-guardian/<control> branch, the hold as a sentence, the proposal, the steps journal, the timeline and links to the finding and the repository Controls /controls, /controls/<id> each assigned control's compliance and coverage; one control's posture by org and lineage, with the versions and revisions each org carries, its compliance over the range, its findings by failing rule and its ten oldest findings Orgs /orgs, /orgs/<org> the orgs tree: each org a row (tracked, compliant, non-compliant, open PRs, parked) that expands (?open=acme,globex) to its repositories in the same grid, with a repository filter over the loaded rows (?q=), a Parked tab (reason and when) and a PR activity tab (open pull requests per org, stale and oldest; needs the Remediation App); cells shade by their share of the measured assignments and the footer sums the visible orgs. One org's baseline against what it added, its controls, its compliance over the range (aggregate=org), its five worst and its exclusions with their reasons Repositories /repositories, /repositories/<id> repositories filtered by name and policy state (?org=, ?q=, ?policy_state=); one repository's controls, each with its bucket, mode and rule results with evidence, its evaluation log and its events, and Re-evaluate History /history compliance over time from the daily snapshots, for every control or one (?control=), over 1, 7, 30 or 90 days (?days=) Policy /policy the active policy version and rollout, each of your orgs' layers (added, replaced, excluded, excluded repositories, repository groups) and the catalogue entries they reference; the enterprise layer only for users who see every org Status /status public service status: no login, no names

Compliance and coverage show no data when there is nothing to measure, never 100%. Evidence is text: its kind, then its fields as key: value lines.

Everything about remediation — the fleet's PR panels, the Findings remediation column, the orgs tree's PR activity, the repository's remediation panels, the Remediations page and its nav count, the status backlog cell — is gated on the Remediation App being installed (the status page's apps). Without it those panels read "Remediation is not enabled on this deployment" rather than an empty state. A hold always reads as a sentence: the repository is at max_open_prs; waits for a slot (pr_cap), a repo-guardian/ branch exists that the bot did not create; rename or delete it to resume (foreign_branch), branch left from a closed PR; delete it to resume (stale_branch), the PR branch conflicts with the default branch and could not be updated (conflict), the Remediation App lacks permission for this change (permission).

On a repository, Remediable rule says whether a rule can be fixed by remediation at all; the facts card's remediable says whether the Remediation App can reach this repository. A no there carries the hint "Remediation App has no access to this repository".

Re-evaluate asks for the repository to be evaluated now. It is hidden for a parked repository, and disappears for the session once the API answers 501, which an API without a Temporal client does (chart value api.temporal).

The header's org scope (?org=) and the range (?days=) follow you from page to page; a view's own filters stay behind. Every table has an Export of the rows it shows as CSV; the findings export pages the API up to 10,000 rows and says when that cap cut it short.

A signed-in user whose groups map to no org sees an "ask for access" page with their name and subject, to quote to an administrator.

docs.title: The status page
docs.text: /status is public: no sign-in, no cookie, and no org, repository or control name. It shows a headline for the overall state, each component (checks, webhooks, discovery, snapshots and each queue's backlog) with its state, fleet compliance as one number with its coverage and 30-day line, an operations strip (repositories evaluated in the last 24 hours of those tracked, overdue evaluations, the newest policy's rollout and the last snapshot, and — with the Remediation App — the remediation backlog), the deployment: its topology and each App's installation and repository counts, and the changelog: the newest five releases from ui/CHANGELOG.yaml, bundled at build time with a running badge on the release this UI ships in, and All releases to GitHub. webhooks is informational and never moves the overall state. It refreshes every 30 seconds.

docs.title: Sessions
docs.text:
• The session lives only in an encrypted, HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite=Lax cookie (__Host-rg_session), split into chunks when large. Page scripts cannot read it, and the browser never sees an access or refresh token.
  • The UI's server refreshes the access token when it is within 60 seconds of expiry. A failed refresh signs you out.
  • A session lasts at most ui.sessionTTL (default 8h), however long the IdP's refresh token lives. Then you sign in again.
  • Sign out revokes the refresh token at the IdP (when it supports RFC 7009), clears the cookie and ends the IdP session.

There is no server-side session store. A copied cookie therefore works until it expires. The 8h cap, revocation on sign-out and key rotation bound that.

docs.title: Rotating session keys
docs.text:
session-keys is a comma-separated list. Each key must be at least 32 bytes. The first key seals new sessions, and any listed key opens existing ones.

  • Routine rotation, no one signed out: prepend a new key, keeping the old one: session-keys: <new>,<old>. Roll the UI. After ui.sessionTTL has passed, remove <old>.
  • Emergency (a key leaked): replace the list with a fresh key alone and roll the UI. Every session is invalid at once and everyone signs in again.
kubectl -n repo-guardian create secret generic repo-guardian-ui \
  --from-literal=oidc-client-secret="$CLIENT_SECRET" \
  --from-literal=session-keys="$(openssl rand -base64 48),$OLD_KEY" \
  --dry-run=client -o yaml | kubectl apply -f -
kubectl -n repo-guardian rollout restart deploy/repo-guardian-ui

docs.title: Security properties
docs.text:
• Text from repositories (paths, file contents, setting values) is rendered as text only. There is no markdown rendering of evidence, and a lint rule bans every HTML sink in the UI's code.
  • PR and repository links are built from the host (ui.githubHost), org, name and number, never copied from evidence, and open with rel="noopener noreferrer".
  • Every response carries Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'self'; connect-src 'self'; frame-ancestors 'none'; script-src 'self', plus nosniff and Referrer-Policy: same-origin.
  • /api/* on the UI host forwards only GET and HEAD, plus the one POST /repositories/<id>/evaluate with a same-origin Origin, only to the api Service. It drops your cookies before forwarding and sends exactly one token: yours if you sent a Bearer, otherwise the session's.
  • The UI pod holds no GitHub, Temporal or database credential.
